# dpi-paper.tex

## Abstract

At Stony Brook, Luca asked me if disintegrations have a generalization where $F:\N\to\M$ is no longer a $*$-homomorphism but a CPU map. It turns out that the answer to this is no! In~[cite:PaBayes], I proved that if $F$ is a CPU map of von Neumann algebras

that has a disintegration, then it is ``almost everywhere'' a $*$-homomorphism. I believe the reason he asked is because he wanted to know if there is a generalization of the modular group flow to situations where you don't necessarily have a subalgebra (when $F$ is a $*$-homomorphism). However, not all is lost! The Bayes' condition provides a generalization of disintegrations that allows $F$ to still be CPU. In the notation of the section below, the Bayes' condition reads $\xi(G(M)N)=\omega(MF(N)),$ where $G:\M\to\N$ is a Bayesian inverse of $(F,\omega,\xi)$. Very recently~[cite:PaRuBayes], Ben and I proved when such a $G$ exists for finite-dimensional $C^*$-algebras. On the other hand, there seems to be a similar statement for normal faithful states in~[cite:An06] involving the modular group. I propose that we try to understand the relationship between all of these perspectives (note: neither the article~[cite:An06] nor any of the articles that cite it have made any connection to Bayes' theorem---this could be a big point to our paper).

Note that $F(\N)$ is now an operator system inside $\M$ (an is a topologically closed vector subspace of a $C^*$-algebra that is closed under the involution $*$ and also contains the identity). I suspect this operator system (or its double commutant) is the proper generalization of the fixed subalgebra under the modular group. Let me outline very specific goals/tasks now.

- Complete our statement and proof relating disintegrations and conditional expectations. First assume $F$ is injective, then drop the condition to see what can be said. Then drop the faithfulness assumption.

-
Ideally, make this article somewhat accessible to physicists, at least those who have read Witten's review~[cite:Wi18]. So review some of the less familiar ideas bringing in finite-dimensional examples for clarity. In particular, review the modular group flow and Takesaki's theorem.

-
Generalize [cite:An06] to allow for non-faithful states. Explain the relationship between that theorem and Bayes's theorem at a level accessible to the operator algebra community. In particular, what does our matrix completion method say in the modular group setting? How are these two results related?

## Definition [label:defn:recoverability]

Let $\A,\B,\C$ be $C^*$-algebras and let $\B\xstoch{F}\A$, $\A\xstoch{\omega}\C$, and $\B\xstoch{\xi}\C$ be UCP. The map $F$ is said to be iff $\xi=\omega\circ F$.
Assuming $F$ is $(\omega,\xi)$-preserving, a UCP $\A\xstoch{G}\B$ is an iff $G$ is $(\xi,\omega)$-preserving.
Assuming $F$ is $(\omega,\xi)$-preserving, a UCP $\A\xstoch{G}\B$ is a of $(F,\omega,\xi)$ iff $\omega(AF(B))=\xi(G(A)B)$ for all $A\in\A$, $B\in\B$. Assuming $F$ is $(\omega,\xi)$-preserving, a UCP $\A\xstoch{G}\B$ is a of $(F,\omega,\xi)$ iff $G$ is $(\omega,\xi)$-preserving and $G\circ F\aeequals{\xi}\id_{\B}$.

Note that the definition of a recovery actually has little to do with the UCP map $F$ in the sense that it only depends on the UCP maps $\omega$ and $\xi$. Also note that $G$ being a Bayesian inverse of $(F,\omega,\xi)$ automatically implies $G$ is $(\omega,\xi)$-recovering. However, being a Bayesian inverse is generally a much stronger condition, even in the commutative setting. A special case of this definition is when $\C=\CC$, which reproduces the notion of state-preserving UCP maps, Bayesian inverses, and disintegrations discussed in earlier sections. The reason for bringing all these definitions to the reader's attention is because they have all been used as different (i.e., inequivalent) definitions of sufficiency in the literature, often in the special case where $\C$ is a commutative $C^*$-algebra. For example, the first part of the next lemma illustrates that our definition of $(\omega,\xi)$ recovery agrees with Petz' definition of sufficiency for a collection of states.

## Lemma [label:lem:pointwiserecovery]

Let $\Theta$ be a finite set, set $\C:=\CC^{\Theta}$, and let $\B\xstoch{F}\A$ and $\A\xstoch{\omega}\C$ be UCP maps. Set $\xi:=\omega\circ F$. For each $\theta\in\Theta$, set $\omega_{\theta}:=ev_{\theta}\circ\omega$, where $ev_{\theta}$ is the evaluation map at $\theta$ sending a function $\varphi$ to $\varphi(\theta)$.

[(a)]

-
An $(\omega,\xi)$-recovery exists if and only if there exists a UCP $\A\xstoch{G}\B$ such that $G$
satisfies $\xi_{\theta}\circ G=\omega_{\theta}$

for all $\theta\in\Theta$.

-
A Bayesian inverse (disintegration) of $(F,\omega,\xi)$ exists if and only if there exists a UCP $\A\xstoch{G}\B$ such that $G$ is a Bayesian inverse (disintegration) of $(F,\omega_{\theta},\xi_{\theta})$ for all $\theta\in\Theta$.

From this, the reader can see that $G$ is an $(\omega,\xi)$-recovery if and only if the channel $F$ is sufficient with respect to the family $\omega$ with respect to the terminology of Petz~[cite:Pe88].

## Proof

[Proof of Lemma~[ref:lem:pointwiserecovery]]
Both follow from the fact that $\{ev_{\theta}\}$ is a separating set of functions on $\Theta$.

The proof suggests an immediate generalization. Recall, a on a $C^*$-algebra $\C$ is a collection of states $\{\zeta_{\theta}\}_{\theta\in\Theta}$ indexed by some set $\Theta$ (which can be taken to be finite if $\C$ is finite-dimensional). Note that every $C^*$-algebra (finite-dimensional or not) admits a separating family of states (the set of all states, for example) .

## Lemma

Let $\B\xstoch{F}\A$ and $\A\xstoch{\omega}\C$ be UCP maps, set $\xi:=\omega\circ F$, and let $\{\zeta_{\theta}\}_{\theta\in\Theta}$ be a separating family of states on $\C$.

[(a)]

-
An $(\omega,\xi)$-recovery exists if and only if there exists a UCP $\A\xstoch{G}\B$ such that $G$
satisfies $\xi_{\theta}\circ G=\omega_{\theta}$

for all $\theta\in\Theta$.

-
A Bayesian inverse (disintegration) of $(F,\omega,\xi)$ exists if and only if there exists a UCP $\A\xstoch{G}\B$ such that $G$ is a Bayesian inverse (disintegration) of $(F,\omega_{\theta},\xi_{\theta})$ for all $\theta\in\Theta$.

The usefulness of this lemma is that one does not gain any new definitions by using an arbitrary finite-dimensional $C^*$-algebra $\C$ in Definition~[ref:defn:recoverability] as opposed to a commutative one. Indeed, if $\C$ is finite-dimensional, then one can always view a separating family of states $\{\zeta_{\theta}\}$ as a UCP map $\C\xstoch{\zeta}\C^{\Theta}$ and a recovery (or Bayesian inverse or disintegration) exists for the original morphisms if and only if it exists for the family. More precisely, the following holds.

## Corollary

Let $\B\xstoch{F}\A$ and $\A\xstoch{\omega}\C$ be UCP maps, set $\xi:=\omega\circ F$, suppose $\C$ is finite-dimensional, and let $\{\zeta_{\theta}\}_{\theta\in\Theta}$ be a finite separating family of states on $\C$, which is viewed as a UCP map $\C\xstoch{\zeta}\CC^{\Theta}$ (such a family necessarily exists).

[(a)]

-
An $(\omega,\xi)$-recovery exists if and only if a $(\zeta\circ\omega,\zeta\circ\xi)$-recovery exists.

-
A Bayesian inverse (disintegration) of $(F,\omega,\xi)$ exists if and only if a Bayesian inverse (disintegration) of $(F,\zeta\circ\omega,\zeta\circ\xi)$ exists.

So if we look at Petz sufficiency with respect to two states, what more restrictions do we get upon also demanding the Bayes condition holds? ## Definition

A (QECC) is a tuple $(\H,\Q,\C,V,\mathcal{E},\mathcal{R})$ consisting of Hilbert spaces $\H$ and $\Q$, a Hilbert subspace $\C\subseteq\H$, an isometry $\Q\xhookrightarrow{V}\H$, and CPTP maps $\mathcal{E},\mathcal{R}:\B(\H)\stoch\B(\H)$ such that $\C:=Im(V)$ and $\mathcal{R}\circ\mathcal{E}\circ\Ad_{P_{\C}}=\Ad_{P_{\C}}$, where $P_{\C}:=V^{\dag}V$ is the orthogonal projection onto the subspace $\C$ inside $\H$. $\mathcal{E}$ is called the , $\C$ the , $V$ the , $\mathcal{R}$ the .

The above definition of a QECC is given in the Schr\"odinger picture for comparison to the standard formulation in the literature. The idea behind this definition is that $\Q$ contains codes that are to be sent across a channel. They are encoded in $\C$ via $V$. The error alters the code and potentially spreads the message across $\H$. The receiver locates which subspace the message is in and performs a specific operation depending on which subspace the code is in. This rectifies the message and pushes it back into the code subspace. To guarantee that the outcome of this procedure produces a density matrix regardless of the input, one should therefore also assume $\Ad_{V^{\dag}}\circ\mathcal{R}$ is trace-preserving.

The of a pair $(\rho,\sigma)$ of density matrices on a Hilbert space $\H$ is given by the formula

$$

\relent{\rho}{\sigma}:=\begin{cases}\tr(\rho\log(\rho))-\tr(\rho\log(\sigma))&\mbox{ if $\rho\preceq\sigma$}\\+\infty&\mbox{ otherwise}
\end{cases}

$$

If $\B(\H)\xstoch{\N}\B(\K)$ is a , i.e., a CPTP map, then the monotonocity theorem states

$$

\relent{\rho}{\sigma}\ge\relent{\N(\rho)}{\N(\sigma)}
\qquad\forall\;\sigma,\rho\in\D(\H),

$$

where $\D(\H)$ denotes the set of density matrices on $\H$.
There are many refinements of this theorem in the literature. Here, we focus on three.
First, in~[cite:Wilde15], Wilde proved

$$

\relent{\rho}{\sigma}\ge\relent{\N(\rho)}{\N(\sigma)}-\log\left(\sup_{t\in\RR} F(\rho,(\R^{P,t}_{\sigma,\N}\circ\N)(\rho))\right),

$$

where

$$

\R^{P,t}_{\sigma,\N}:=\mathfrak{m}^{-t}_{\sigma}\circ\R^{P}_{\sigma,\N}\circ\mathfrak{m}^{t}_{\N(\sigma)}

$$

is the and

$$

\R^{P}_{\sigma,\N}:=\Ad_{\sigma^{1/2}}\circ \N^{*}\circ\Ad_{\widehat{\N(\sigma)}^{1/2}}

$$

is the .
Note that the modular actions are defined using the support since the density matrices need not be invertible and the pseudoinverse of these density matrices is used (cf.\ Section~[ref:sec:cebimgnfs]).
In~[cite:JRSWW16,JRSWW18], Junge et.\ al.\ obtained a slightly different version of this monotonicity theorem, which is given by

$$

\relent{\rho}{\sigma}\ge\relent{\N(\rho)}{\N(\sigma)}-\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\log\left( F(\rho,(\R^{P,t/2}_{\sigma,\N}\circ\N)(\rho))\right)\beta_{0}(t)\,dt,

$$

where $\beta_{0}$ is the probability density function on $\RR$ given by

$$

\RR\ni t\mapsto \beta_{0}(t):=\frac{\pi}{2[\cosh(\pi t)+1]}.

$$

However, these theorems do not provide explicit recovery maps satisfying a similar inequality without either taking an optimization or some averaging procedure. It would be convenient if one could find an explicit recovery map satisfying a similar bound. Such a result was achieved by Junge et.\ al.\ in~[cite:JRSWW16,JRSWW18].
They proved that there exists a CPTP map $\B(\K)\xstoch{\R}\B(\H)$ such that

$$

\relent{\rho}{\sigma}\ge\relent{\N(\rho)}{\N(\sigma)}-\log F(\rho,(\R\circ\N)(\rho))
\qquad\forall\;\rho\in\D(\H).

$$

Since $\sigma$ and $\N(\sigma)$ need not be invertible, $\R^{P,t}_{\sigma,\N}$ need not be trace-preserving. So to obtain a trace-preserving map $\R$ as in this inequality, Junge et al.~[cite:JRSWW16] let $\nu$ be any density matrix on $\H$ and they set

$$

\B(\K)\ni B\mapsto\R(B):=\left(\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\R^{P,t/2}_{\sigma,\N}(B)\beta_{0}(t)\,dt\right)+\tr(P_{\N(\sigma)}^{\perp}B)\nu.

$$

Two points are worth mentioning. First, the choice of $\nu$ is quite arbitrary, and one wonders if there is a more systematic choice. This arbitrary choice was made because the Petz recovery map (and its rotated variants) contains no information off the supports of the density matrices involved. Second, the assignment

$$

\B(\K)\ni B\mapsto\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\R^{P,t/2}_{\sigma,\N}(B)\beta_{0}(t)\,dt

$$

is a non-negative combination of CP maps, and is hence CP. However, it is not clear if a more explicit expression is available.

The Bayes condition provides a solution to both of these points. It provides additional information off these supports, and the integral expression simplifies.

## Lemma [label:lem:ACimpliesRPetzisPetz]

Set $\B:=\B(\K)$, $\A:=\B(\H)$, and $\omega:=\tr(\sigma\;\cdot)$. Let $\A\xstoch{\N}\B$ be a CPTP map with UCP dual $\B\xstoch{\N^{*}}\A$. Set $\xi:=\omega\circ\N^{*}=\tr(\N(\sigma)\;\cdot\;)$. Suppose a Bayesian inverse for $(\N^*,\omega,\xi)$ exists. Then

$$

\R^{P,t}_{\sigma,\N}=\R^{P}_{\sigma,\N}\qquad\forall\;t\in\RR.

$$

In particular,

$$

\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\R^{P,t/2}_{\sigma,\N}(B)\beta_{0}(t)\,dt
=\R^{P}_{\sigma,\N}(B)
\qquad\forall\;B\in\B.

$$

## Proof

If a Bayesian inverse exists, then

$$

\Ad_{P_{\sigma}}\circ\N^{*}\circ\mathfrak{m}^{t}_{\N(\sigma)}=\mathfrak{m}^{t}_{\sigma}\circ\N^{*}\circ\Ad_{P_{\N(\sigma)}}\qquad\forall\;t\in\RR

$$

by the work of Accardi and Cecchini~[cite:AcCe82] (cf.\ Section~[ref:sec:cebimgnfs] above).

Hence, the rotated Petz recovery map equals

$$

\begin{split}
\R^{P,t}_{\sigma,\N}
&=\mathfrak{m}^{-t}_{\sigma}\circ \Ad_{\sigma^{1/2}}\circ\N^*\circ\Ad_{\widehat{\N(\sigma)}^{1/2}}\circ\mathfrak{m}^{t}_{\N(\sigma)}\\
&=\Ad_{\sigma^{1/2}}\circ\mathfrak{m}^{-t}_{\sigma}\circ\Ad_{P_{\sigma}}\circ\N^{*}\circ\mathfrak{m}^{t}_{\N(\sigma)}\circ\circ\Ad_{\widehat{\N(\sigma)}^{1/2}}\\
&=\Ad_{\sigma^{1/2}}\circ\mathfrak{m}^{-t}_{\sigma}\circ\mathfrak{m}^{t}_{\sigma}\circ\N^{*}\circ\Ad_{P_{\N(\sigma)}}\circ\Ad_{\widehat{\N(\sigma)}^{1/2}}\\
&=\Ad_{\sigma^{1/2}}\circ\N^{*}\circ\Ad_{\widehat{\N(\sigma)}^{1/2}},
\end{split}

$$

which is the usual Petz recovery map.

An explicit rewriting of the formula for the rotated Petz recovery map in terms of density matrices is

$$

\R^{P,t}_{\sigma,\N}(B)=\sigma^{-it+\frac{1}{2}}\mathcal{N}^*\left(\widehat{\N(\sigma)}^{\,it-\frac{1}{2}}B\widehat{\N(\sigma)}^{-it-\frac{1}{2}}\right)\sigma^{it+\frac{1}{2}}.

$$

Furthermore, an immediate consequence of Lemma~[ref:lem:ACimpliesRPetzisPetz] is $\R^{P,t}_{\sigma,\N}=\R^{P,s}_{\sigma,\N}$ for all $t,s\in\R$. Therefore, putting these two facts together show that

$$

\R^{P}_{\sigma,\N}(B)=\sigma^{z}\mathcal{N}^*\left(\widehat{\N(\sigma)}^{-z}B\widehat{\N(\sigma)}^{\,z-1}\right)\sigma^{1-z}

$$

for all $z\in\CC$.

## Corollary [label:cor:Jungeinequalityrealization]

Using the same notation and under the same assumptions as in Lemma~[ref:lem:ACimpliesRPetzisPetz], let $G$ denote a Bayesian inverse of $(\N^*,\omega,\xi)$. Then

$$

\relent{\rho}{\sigma}\ge\relent{\N(\rho)}{\N(\sigma)}-\log F(\rho,(G^*\circ\N)(\rho))
\qquad\forall\;\rho\in\D(\H).

$$

Thus, the Accardi--Cecchini condition allows one to provide an explicit CPTP recovery map that agrees with the Petz recovery map on the supported corner, which means $G^*\circAd_{P_{\xi}}=\R_{\sigma,\N}^{P}$. Notice, however, that a Bayesian inverse is uniquely specified on two other corners, and sometimes even outside on the support of the orthogonal complement, but this is not true of the Petz recovery map. In particular, $G$ does not equal the Petz recovery map. Therefore, the converse of Lemma~[ref:lem:ACimpliesRPetzisPetz] does not hold in general. These statements are made more precise in the following.

## Proposition

Let $G$ denote a Bayesian inverse of $(\N^*,\omega,\xi)$, as in Corollary~[ref:cor:Jungeinequalityrealization], but where $\H=\CC^{m}$ and $\K:=\CC^{n}$ with $m,n\in\NN$. Then

$$
P_{\xi}G(A)P_{\xi}&=(\R^{P}_{\sigma,\N})^*,
& & P_{\xi}G(A)P_{\xi}^{\perp}=\widehat{\N(\sigma)}\N(\sigma A) P_{\xi}^{\perp},\text{ and }\\
P_{\xi}^{\perp}G(A)P_{\xi}&=P_{\xi}^{\perp}\N(A \sigma) \widehat{\N(\sigma)}
&&
\quad
$$

for all $A\in\A$. In particular, if $\xi$ is faithful, then $G^*=\R^{P}_{\sigma,\N}$.

There are other important inequalities involving recovery maps and relative entropy in the classical setting. Let us review the main one that will concern us moving forward.

## Theorem [label:thm:relentandBayes]

Let $X$ and $Y$ be finite sets, let $p$ be a probability measure on $X$, and let $X\xstoch{f}Y$ be a stochastic map. Let $f\circ p$ denote the pushforward of $p$ along $f$.

Then there exists a probability-preserving stochastic map $(Y,f\circ p)\xstoch{g}(X,p)$ such that

$$
\relent{q}{p}-\relent{f\circ q}{f\circ p}\ge \relent{q}{g\circ f\circ q}
\qquad\forall\left(\{\bullet\}\xstoch{q}X\right).
$$

Second, one such $g$ is defined by the Bayes' condition; namely,
it is given by

$$

g_{xy}:=\frac{f_{yx} p_{x}}{(f\circ p)_{y}}\qquad\forall (x,y)\in X\times(Y\setminus N_{f\circ p}).

$$

Finally, if $f$ is deterministic, then this inequality becomes an equality with such a choice of $g$.

## Proof

The first claim follows from the calculation

$$

\begin{split}
\relent{q}{p}-\relent{q}{g\circ f\circ q}&=\sum_{x}\Big(q_{x}\log(g\circ f\circ q)_{x}-q_{x}\log p_{x}\Big)\\
&=\sum_{x}q_{x}\log\left(\frac{(g\circ f\circ q)_{x}}{p_{x}}\right)\quad\text{ by properties of $\log$}\\
&=\sum_{x}q_{x}\log\left(\sum_{y}g_{xy}\frac{(f\circ q)_{y}}{p_{x}}\right)\quad\text{ by definition of composition}\\
&=\sum_{x}q_{x}\log\left(\sum_{y}f_{yx}\frac{(f\circ q)_{y}}{(f\circ p)_{y}}\right)\quad\text{ by Bayes' formula for $g$}\\
&\ge\sum_{x}q_{x}\sum_{y}f_{yx}\log\left(\frac{(f\circ q)_{y}}{(f\circ p)_{y}}\right)\quad\text{ by concavity of $\log$}\\
&=\sum_{y}(f\circ q)_{y}\log\left(\frac{(f\circ q)_{y}}{(f\circ p)_{y}}\right)\quad\text{ by definition of composition}\\
&=\relent{f\circ q}{f\circ p}\quad\text{ by properties of $\log$}
\end{split}

$$

It has been a long-standing open problem to prove quantum analogues of Equation~([ref:eqn:relativeentropyrecoveryinequality]) (see for example the discussions around Equation (1.13) in~[cite:CaVe20] and Sections 5 and 6 of~[cite:LiWi18]). To precisely state this inequality, let $\M_{n}(\CC)\xstoch{F}\M_{m}(\CC)$ be a CPU map, and let $\rho$ be a density matrix on $\CC^{m}$. Then does there exist a CPTP map $\M_{n}(\CC)\xstoch{R}\M_{m}(\CC)$ such that $RF^*\rho=\rho$ and

[equation:eqn:qrelativeentropyrecoveryinequality]
$$
\relent{\sigma}{\rho}-\relent{F^*\sigma}{F^*\rho}\ge\relent{\sigma}{RF^*\sigma}
$$

for all density matrices $\sigma\preceq\rho$ on $\CC^{m}$?
Partial results in this direction include Theorem 4 in~[cite:DuWi16] which replace the relative entropy on the right-hand-side of ([ref:eqn:qrelativeentropyrecoveryinequality]) with an infimum over $0$-Renyi divergences and over all rotated Petz recovery maps. Another partial result is one where the right-hand-side of ([ref:eqn:qrelativeentropyrecoveryinequality]) is replaced with the measured relative entropy~[cite:SuBeTo17].
In fact, it is known that the inequality~([ref:eqn:qrelativeentropyrecoveryinequality])
is false in the quantum setting even when using the Petz recovery map or its rotated (swivelled) variants for $R$ (see~[cite:LiWi18] and references therein for details). We will partially illustrate this explicitly with analytic (as opposed to numerical) counter-examples. Afterwards, we will find sufficient conditions for the inequality to be satisfied. We will also prove a quantum analogue of Theorem~[ref:thm:relentandBayes]. But before that, first note that the inequality~([ref:eqn:qrelativeentropyrecoveryinequality]) can be rewritten as

[equation:eqn:qrelativeentropyrecoveryinequalityrewrite]
$$
f(\rho,F,R,\sigma):=-\tr\left(\sigma\log\rho\right)-\tr\left(F^*\sigma\log F^*\sigma\right)+\tr\left(F^*\sigma\log F^*\rho\right)+\tr\left(\sigma\log RF^*\sigma\right)\ge0.
$$

## Example

Take $m=4$ and $n=2$ and let $\M_{2}\xrightarrow{F}\M_{4}$ be the $*$-homomorphism taking $B$ to $F(B):=\mathds{1}_{2}\otimes B$. This is a deterministic map, and its Hilbert--Schmidt dual is the partial trace. Consider the two-parameter family of density matrices given by

$$

\begin{split}
(0,1)\times(0,1)&\to\M_{4}(\CC)\\
(p,q)&\mapsto\rho(p,q):=\begin{bmatrix}qp&0&0&0\\0&(1-q)(1-p)&0&0\\0&0&(1-q)p&0\\0&0&0&q(1-p)\end{bmatrix}
\end{split}

$$

and consider the one-parameter family of density matrices given by

$$

\begin{split}
(0,1/2)&\to\M_{4}(\CC)\\
r&\mapsto\sigma(r):=\frac{1}{4}\begin{bmatrix}1&2r&0&0\\2r&1&0&0\\0&0&1&2r\\0&0&2r&1\end{bmatrix}.
\end{split}

$$

Then

$$

F^*\rho=\begin{bmatrix}p_{1}+p_{3}&0\\0&p_{2}+p_{4}\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}p&0\\0&1-p\end{bmatrix}
\quad\text{ and }\quad
F^*\sigma=\begin{bmatrix}1/2&r\\r&1/2\end{bmatrix}.

$$

We can now explicitly compute the first three terms in~([ref:eqn:qrelativeentropyrecoveryinequalityrewrite]). They are

$$

\tr(\sigma\log\rho)=-\frac{1}{2}\log\big(q(1-q)p(1-p)\big),

$$

$$

\tr(F^*\sigma\log F^*\sigma)=\frac{1}{2}\Big((1+2r)\log(1+2r)+(1-2r)\log(1-2r)-\log4\Big),

$$

and

$$

\tr(F^*\sigma\log F^*\rho)=\frac{1}{2}\log\big(p(1-p)\big).

$$

For the recovery map $R$, we shall take the one-parameter family of rotated Petz recovery maps $\mathcal{R}^{P,t}_{\rho,F^*}$. In our case, this is not difficult to compute explicitly on $F^*\sigma$. The result is

$$

\begin{split}
\mathcal{R}^{P,t}_{\rho,F^*}\left(F^*\sigma\right)
&=\rho^{\frac{1}{2}-it}\left[\mathds{1}_{2}\otimes\left((F^*\rho)^{-\frac{1}{2}+it}(F^*\sigma)(F^*\rho)^{-\frac{1}{2}-it}\right)\right]\rho^{\frac{1}{2}+it}\\
&=\begin{bmatrix}
\frac{q}{2}&rq^{\frac{1}{2}-it}(1-q)^{\frac{1}{2}+it}&0&0\\
rq^{\frac{1}{2}+it}(1-q)^{\frac{1}{2}-it}&\frac{1-q}{2}&0&0\\
0&0&\frac{1-q}{2}&rq^{\frac{1}{2}+it}(1-q)^{\frac{1}{2}-it}\\
0&0&rq^{\frac{1}{2}-it}(1-q)^{\frac{1}{2}+it}&\frac{q}{2}
\end{bmatrix}
.
\end{split}

$$

Therefore,

$$

\begin{split}
\tr&\left(\sigma\log \left(\mathcal{R}^{P,t}_{\rho,F^*}\left(F^*\sigma\right)\right)\right)
=\frac{1}{2}\log\left(\frac{(1-4r^2)q(1-q)}{4}\right)\\
&\qquad\qquad+8r^2\cos\left(\frac{1-q}{q}t\right)\sqrt{\frac{q(1-q)}{1-4(1-4r^2)q(1-q)}}
arctanh\sqrt{1-4(1-4r^2)q(1-q)}
\end{split}.

$$

Since this expression is maximized as a function of $t$ when $t=\frac{2\pi q}{1-q}n$ for $n\in\ZZ$, it suffices to consider the largest value, which occurs when $t=0$ for example. Hence, it suffices to consider the ordinary Petz recovery map instead of the rotated ones when maximizing $f\big(\rho,F,\mathcal{R}^{P,t}_{\rho,F^*},\sigma\big)$.
From this, we obtain

$$

\begin{split}

f\left(\rho,F,\mathcal{R}^{P}_{\rho,F^*},\sigma\right)&=-r\log\left(\frac{1+2r}{1-2r}\right)+8r^2\sqrt{\frac{q(1-q)}{1-4(1-4r^2)q(1-q)}}
arctanh\sqrt{1-4(1-4r^2)q(1-q)}
\end{split}

$$

which satisfies $f\left(\rho,F,\mathcal{R}^{P}_{\rho,F^*},\sigma\right)\le0$ for all values of the parameters and satisfies $f\left(\rho,F,\mathcal{R}^{P}_{\rho,F^*},\sigma\right)=0$ when either $r=0$ or $q=\frac{1}{2}$. The same holds for all the rotated Petz recovery maps. Hence, these families of density matrices violate the inequality~([ref:eqn:qrelativeentropyrecoveryinequality]) using the rotated Petz recovery maps except for very special values of the parameters. If $r=0$, then the density matrix $F^*\sigma$ is diagonal, and the inequality is already known to hold in this case (cf.~[cite:LiWi18]). However, if $q=\frac{1}{2}$, we also see that the inequality holds for all values of $r$. Note that because $F$ is deterministic, when the inequality does hold, it is an equality, consistent with the classical setting.

The conditions for when the equality holds for all density matrices $\sigma$ in the previous example can be generalized as follows.

## Theorem [label:thm:ineqholdsfordisints]

Let $\M_{n}(\CC)\xrightarrow{F}\M_{m}(\CC)$ be a (unital) $*$-homomorphism and let $\rho$ be a density matrix on $\CC^{m}$. Suppose a Bayesian inverse (i.e., disintegration in this case) $G$ of $(F,\rho,F^*\rho)$ exists. Then

$$

\relent{\sigma}{\rho}-\relent{F^*\sigma}{F^*\rho}=\relent{\sigma}{G^*F^*\sigma}

$$

for all density matrices $\sigma\preceq\rho$ on $\CC^{m}$.

## Proof

Since $F$ is a unital $*$-homomorphism, there exists a $p\in\NN$ such that $m=np$. For convenience of notation later, set $\B:=\M_{n}(\CC)$, $\C:=\M_{p}(\CC)$, so that $\A:=\M_{m}(\C)$ can be written as $\A=\C\otimes\B$. In this way, $F^*=\tr_{\C}$ is the partial trace over $\C$.

Now, since $(F,\rho,F^*\rho)$ has a disintegration, there exists another density matrix $\tau\in\M_{p}(\CC)$ such that $\rho=\tau\otimes F^*\rho$. For the remainder of this calculation, let $P_{\sigma}$ be the support projection of $\sigma$ and similarly for the other density matrices.
Then

$$

\begin{split}
\tr(\sigma\log\rho)&=

\tr\left(\sigma\log\left(\tau\otimes F^*\rho\right)\right)\\
&=\tr\Big(\sigma P_{\sigma}\log\left(\tau\otimes F^*\rho\right)P_{\sigma}\Big)\\
&=\tr\Big(\sigma \big[P_{\sigma}\left(\log\tau\otimes\mathds{1}_{n}\right)P_{\sigma}+P_{\sigma}\left(\mathds{1}_{p}\otimes\log(F^*\rho)\right)P_{\sigma}\big]\Big)\\
&=\tr\big(\sigma(\log\tau\otimes\mathds{1}_{n})\big)+\tr\big(\sigma(\mathds{1}_{p}\otimes\log(F^*\rho))\big)\\
&=\tr\big(\tr_{\B}(\sigma)\log(\tau)\big)+\tr\big(\tr_{\C}(\sigma)\log(F^*\rho)\big)\\
&=\tr\big(\tr_{\B}(\sigma)\log(\tau)\big)+\tr\big(F^*\sigma\log (F^*\rho)\big).
\end{split}

$$

Note that the splitting of the logarithm in the third equality into two terms is allowed because $P_{\sigma}\le P_{\rho}=P_{\tau}\otimes P_{F^*\rho}$. The second last equality follows from the properties of trace and partial trace. The last equality follows from the fact that $F^*=\tr_{\C}$. A similar calculation shows

$$

\tr\big(\sigma\log(G^*F^*\sigma)\big)=\tr\big(\sigma\log(\tau\otimes F^*\sigma)\big)=\tr\big(\tr_{\B}(\sigma)\log(\tau)\big)+\tr\big(F^*\sigma\log(F^*\sigma)\big).

$$

Therefore, the difference $f(\rho,F,G^*,\sigma)$ is

$$

f(\rho,F,G^*,\sigma)=-\tr\left(\sigma\log\rho\right)-\tr\left(F^*\sigma\log F^*\sigma\right)+\tr\left(F^*\sigma\log F^*\rho\right)+\tr\left(\sigma\log RF^*\sigma\right)=0

$$

as needed.

## Remark

Note that $G^*$ in Theorem~[ref:thm:ineqholdsfordisints] agrees with the Petz recovery map when $F^*\rho$ is invertible.

Since disintegrations are special kinds of Bayesian inverses, Theorem~[ref:thm:ineqholdsfordisints] suggests the conjecture that inequality~([ref:eqn:qrelativeentropyrecoveryinequality]) might hold more generally for arbitrary CPU maps $F$ provided that a Bayesian inverse of $(F,\rho,F^*\rho)$ exists. A Bayesian inverse would then fill the role of the recovery map $R$ in the inequality~([ref:eqn:qrelativeentropyrecoveryinequality]).

### Some useful operator inequalities

The following theorem is a result of Davis~[cite:Da57]. It can be viewed as a non-commutative Jensen inequality. It is sometimes called the Choi--Davis--Jensen inequality.

## Theorem [label:thm:ChoiDavisJensen]

Let $F:\B\to\B(\H)$ be a CP map of $C^*$-algebras, let $\varphi$ be an operator convex function defined on some real interval $J$ with $0\in J$ and such that $\varphi(0)=0$, and let $B\in\B$ with spectrum contained in $J$. Then

$$

\varphi\big(F(B)\big)\le F\big(\varphi(A)\big)

$$

## Corollary

Let $F:\B\to\B(\H)=:\A$ be CPU map and let $B\in\B$ be positive. Then

$$

\log\big(F(B)\big)\ge F\big(\log(B)\big).

$$

Note that the Choi--Davis--Jensen inequality cannot be directly applied to the logarithm because $0$ is not in its domain. Nevertheless, the statement holds.

## Proof

For each $\epsilon>0$, define $\varphi_{\epsilon}:[0,\infty)\to\RR$ by

$$

[0,\infty)\ni t\xmapsto{\varphi_{\epsilon}}-\log\left(\frac{t+\epsilon}{\epsilon}\right).

$$

Then $\varphi_{\epsilon}$ is operator convex (cf.\ [cite:Ch15] for example) and satisfies $\varphi_{\epsilon}(0)=0$. Hence, for any $B\ge0$ in $\B$,

$$

\varphi_{\epsilon}\big(F(B)\big)\le F\big(\varphi_{\epsilon}(B)\big)

$$

by the Choi--Davis--Jensen inequality. Unravelling this gives

$$

\log(\epsilon)1_{\A}-\log\big(F(B)+\epsilon1_{\A}\big)\le \log(\epsilon)F(1_{\B})-F\big(\log(B+\epsilon1_{\B})\big).

$$

By unitality of $F$, we obtain

$$

-\log\big(F(B)+\epsilon1_{\A}\big)\le -F\big(\log(B+\epsilon1_{\B})\big).

$$

By continuity and the validity of this inequality for all $\epsilon>0$, we obtain

$$

-\log\big(F(B)\big)\le -F\big(\log(B)\big).

$$

which is equivalent to the claim.

### When trace-decreasing UCP maps are Bayesian invertible with respect to the tracial state

## Lemma [label:lem:imageofchannel]

If $\A:=\matr_{d}(\CC)\xstoch{\mathcal{N}}\matr_{d'}(\CC)=:\B$ is a positive map and if $P$ denotes the support projection of $\mathcal{N}(\mathds{1}_{d})$, then $\mathcal{N}(\A)\subseteq P\B P$.

## Proof

Since $\rho\le\lVert\rho\rVert\mathds{1}_{d}$ for all positive $\rho\in\matr_{d}(\CC)$, one concludes $\mathcal{N}(\rho)\le\lVert\rho\rVert\mathcal{N}(\mathds{1}_{d})\le\lVert\rho\rVert\lVert\mathcal{N}(\mathds{1}_{d})\rVert P$ because $P$ is the unit of $P\B P$. Hence, $\mathcal{N}(\rho)\in P\B P$. Since every $A\in\matr_{d}(\CC)$ is a linear combination of four positive elements, $\mathcal{N}(A)\in P\B P$, and the conclusion follows.

## Lemma [label:lem:CPTPSUmaps]

Let $d,d'\in\NN$ and
let $\A:=\matr_{d}(\CC)\xstoch{\mathcal{N}}\matr_{d'}(\CC)=:\B$ be a CPTP map. Then the following facts hold.

-
If $\mathcal{N}$ is, in addition, sub-unital, then the dimension of the codomain of $\mathcal{N}$ is at least that of the domain, i.e., $d'\ge d$.

-
If $\mathcal{N}$ is, in addition, sub-unital, and if $d'=d$, then $\mathcal{N}$ is unital; equivalently, the totally mixed density matrix $\frac{1}{d}\mathds{1}_{d}$ is invariant under $\mathcal{N}$.

-
If $d'\ge d$ and $\mathcal{N}$ preserves the totally mixed uniform density matrix, i.e.,
$\mathcal{N}(\frac{1}{d}\mathds{1}_{d})=\frac{1}{d'}\mathds{1}_{d'}$, then $\mathcal{N}$ is sub-unital. In particular, if $d=d'$, then $\mathcal{N}$ is unital.

## Proof

you found me!

-
Sub-unitality says $\mathcal{N}(\mathds{1}_{d})\le\mathds{1}_{d'}$. Applying the trace to both sides and using the trace-preserving assumption on $\mathcal{N}$ gives $d\le d'$, which proves the claim.

-
The Hilbert--Schmidt norm gives

$$
0&\le\big\lVert\mathds{1}_{d'}-\mathcal{N}(\mathds{1}_{d})\big\rVert_{HS}^2=\tr\Big(\big(\mathds{1}_{d'}-\mathcal{N}(\mathds{1}_{d})\big)^{\dag}\big(\mathds{1}_{d'}-\mathcal{N}(\mathds{1}_{d})\big)\Big)\\
&=\tr\Big(\mathds{1}_{d'}-\mathcal{N}(\mathds{1}_{d})-\mathcal{N}(\mathds{1}_{d})^{\dag}+\mathcal{N}(\mathds{1}_{d})^{\dag}\mathcal{N}(\mathds{1}_{d})\Big)\\
&=d'-d-d+\tr\Big(\mathcal{N}(\mathds{1}_{d})^{\dag}\mathcal{N}(\mathds{1}_{d})\Big)\\
&\le d'-2d+\tr\Big(\mathcal{N}\big(\mathds{1}_{d}^{\dag}\mathds{1}_{d}\big)\Big)\\
&=d'-2d+d=d'-d=0.
$$

The trace-preservation property of $\mathcal{N}$ was used in the third and fifth lines.
The inequality in the fourth line follows from the Kadison--Schwarz inequality, which uses the sub-unitality of $\mathcal{N}$.
The fact that $d'=d$ was used in the last equality.
Since the Hilbert--Schmidt norm is non-degenerate, this proves $\mathds{1}_{d}=\mathcal{N}(\mathds{1}_{d})$.

-
By assumption $\mathcal{N}(\mathds{1}_{d})=\frac{d}{d'}\mathds{1}_{d'}\le\mathds{1}_{d'}$ since $d\le d'$. The second claim follows from this and the second part of this lemma.

## Remark [label:rmk:CPTPSUBayesex]

Using the notation from Lemma~[ref:lem:CPTPSUmaps], if $d'>d$, it need not be the case that $\mathcal{N}(\mathds{1}_{d})$ is equal to a rank $d$ projection. A counter-example is the CPTP map given by sending $A\in\matr_{d}(\CC)$ to

$$

\mathcal{N}(A)=\frac{1-\epsilon}{d'}\tr(A)\mathds{1}_{d'}+\epsilon VAV^{\dag},

$$

where $\epsilon\in(0,1)$ and $V:\CC^{d}\to\CC^{d'}$ is an isometry. With this example, the image of $\mathds{1}_{d}$ is not a projection. Note that this map is indeed sub-unital because

$$

\N(\mathds{1}_{d})
=\frac{(1-\epsilon)d}{d'}\mathds{1}_{d'}+\epsilon VV^{\dag}
\le\frac{(1-\epsilon)d}{d'}\mathds{1}_{d'}+\epsilon\mathds{1}_{d'}=\frac{d+\epsilon(d'-d)}{d'}\mathds{1}_{d'}
\le\frac{d}{d'}\mathds{1}_{d'}\le\mathds{1}_{d'}.

$$

The Hilbert--Schmidt dual of this map is given by

$$

\mathcal{N}^{*}(B)=\frac{1-\epsilon}{d}\tr(B)\mathds{1}_{d}+\epsilon V^{\dag}BV

$$

for all $B\in\matr_{d'}(\CC)$.
Meanwhile, to compute the associated Petz recovery map using the uniform prior $\rho=\frac{\mathds{1}_{d}}{d}$, we first compute the inverse of

$$

\N(\rho)=\frac{1-\epsilon}{d'}\mathds{1}_{d'}+\frac{\epsilon}{d}VV^{\dag},

$$

which is

$$

\N(\rho)^{-1}
=\frac{d'}{1-\epsilon}\left(\mathds{1}_{d'}-\frac{\epsilon d'}{(1-\epsilon)d+\epsilon d'}VV^{\dag}\right).

$$

Using this, we can obtain the (unique positive) square-root explicitly, and the result is

$$

\N(\rho)^{-1/2}=\sqrt{\frac{d'}{1-\epsilon}}\left(\mathds{1}_{d'}+\left(-1+\sqrt{\frac{(1-\epsilon)d}{(1-\epsilon)d+\epsilon d'}}\right)VV^{\dag}\right).

$$

Putting this together, the Petz recovery map is given by

$$

\begin{split}
\mathcal{R}^{P}_{\rho,\mathcal{N}}(B)&=\left(\Ad_{\rho^{1/2}}\circ\N^{*}\circ\Ad_{\N(\rho)^{-1/2}}\right)(B)\\
&=\left(\frac{d'}{d}\right)^{2}\left(\frac{\tr(B)}{d'}-\frac{\epsilon}{(1-\epsilon)d+\epsilon d'}\tr\big(V^{\dag}BV\big)\right)\mathds{1}_{d}+\frac{\epsilon d'}{(1-\epsilon)d+\epsilon d'}V^{\dag}BV
\end{split}

$$

for all $B\in\matr_{d'}(\CC)$.
Note that the Petz recovery map does not in general equal $\N^*$ in this example, but the two are equal when $d=d'$ (since then $V$ is a unitary so that $\tr(V^{\dag}BV)=\tr(B)$ for all $B$).

In the next theorem, we recall the main result of Buscemi, Das, and Wilde~[cite:BDW16].

## Theorem [label:thm:BDWmain]

Let $\matr_{d}(\CC)\xstoch{\mathcal{N}}\matr_{d'}(\CC)$ be a positive and trace-preserving map. Then

$$

H\big(\mathcal{N}(\sigma)\big)-H(\sigma)\ge \relent{\sigma}{(\mathcal{N}^*\circ\mathcal{N})(\sigma)}

$$

for all density matrices $\sigma\in\matr_{d}(\CC)$.
In particular, setting $\rho:=\frac{1}{d}\mathds{1}_{d}$ and $\matr_{d'}(\CC)\xstoch{\mathcal{R}^{\BDW}_{\rho,\N}}\matr_{d}(\CC)$ to be the map

$$

\matr_{d'}(\CC)\ni B\xmapsto{\mathcal{R}^{\BDW}_{\rho,\N}} \mathcal{N}^*(B)+\Big(\tr(B)-\tr\big(\mathcal{N}^*(B)\big)\Big)\tau,

$$

where $\tau$ is some density matrix $\matr_{d}(\CC)$, then $\mathcal{R}^{\BDW}_{\rho,\N}$ is positive, trace-preserving, and satisfies

$$

H\big(\mathcal{N}(\sigma)\big)-H(\sigma)\ge \relent{\sigma}{(\mathcal{R}^{\BDW}_{\rho,\N}\circ\mathcal{N})(\sigma)}

$$

for all density matrices $\sigma\in\matr_{d}(\CC)$.

## Proof

This is Theorem~1 of~[cite:BDW16].

It was claimed in~[cite:BDW16] that this strengthens the DPI.
We make this more explicit by deriving the following result.

## Corollary [label:cor:BDWSDPI]

Let $\matr_{d}(\CC)\xstoch{\mathcal{N}}\matr_{d}(\CC)$ be a positive, trace-preserving map, and sub-unital map. Set $\rho:=\frac{1}{d}\mathds{1}_{d}$.
Then

$$

\relent{\sigma}{\rho}-\relent{\mathcal{N}(\sigma)}{\mathcal{N}(\rho)}-\relent{\sigma}{(\mathcal{R}^{\BDW}_{\rho,\N}\circ\mathcal{N})(\sigma)}\ge0

$$

for all density matrices $\sigma$ in $\matr_{d}(\CC)$. Here, $\mathcal{R}^{\BDW}_{\rho,\N}$ is the recovery map from Theorem~[ref:thm:BDWmain].

## Proof

For reference, set

$$

SDPI[\sigma,\rho,\mathcal{N},\mathcal{R}^{\BDW}_{\rho,\N}]:=\relent{\sigma}{\rho}-\relent{\mathcal{N}(\sigma)}{\mathcal{N}(\rho)}-\relent{\sigma}{(\mathcal{R}^{\BDW}_{\rho,\N}\circ\mathcal{N})(\sigma)}.

$$

We also compute the general expressions for the relative entropies in the stated inequality without assuming $\matr_{d}(\CC)\xstoch{\mathcal{N}}\matr_{d'}(\CC)$ is unital and without assuming $d'=d$. First,

$$

\relent{\sigma}{\rho}
=\tr\big(\sigma\ln(\sigma)\big)-\tr\left(\sigma\ln\left(\frac{1}{d}\mathds{1}_{d}\right)\right)
=-H(\sigma)+\ln(d).

$$

Similarly,

$$

\relent{\mathcal{N}(\sigma)}{\mathcal{N}(\rho)}
=H\big(\mathcal{N}(\sigma)\big)-\ln(d)+\tr\Big(\mathcal{N}(\sigma)\ln\big(\mathcal{N}(\mathds{1}_{d})\big)\Big)

$$

since $\mathcal{N}$ is trace-preserving. Hence,

$$

\relent{\sigma}{\rho}-\relent{\mathcal{N}(\sigma)}{\mathcal{N}(\rho)}
=H\big(\mathcal{N}(\sigma)\big)-H(\sigma)+\tr\Big(\mathcal{N}(\sigma)\ln\big(\mathcal{N}(\mathds{1}_{d})\big)\Big).

$$

Now, since $d'=d$, Lemma~[ref:lem:CPTPSUmaps] shows that $\mathcal{N}$ is unital. Hence,

$$

\relent{\sigma}{\rho}-\relent{\mathcal{N}(\sigma)}{\mathcal{N}(\rho)}
=H\big(\mathcal{N}(\sigma)\big)-H(\sigma).

$$

Again, since $\mathcal{N}$ is unital, then $\mathcal{N}^*$ is trace-preserving, and $\mathcal{R}^{\BDW}_{\rho,\N}=\mathcal{N}^*$. By Theorem~[ref:thm:BDWmain], the claimed inequality holds.

However, if the codomain of $\mathcal{N}$ is $\matr_{d'}(\CC)$, with $d'\ne d$,
then the conclusion of Corollary~[ref:cor:BDWSDPI] no longer holds with the recovery map $\mathcal{R}^{\BDW}_{\rho,\N}$ from Theorem~[ref:thm:BDWmain]. Before we provide an explicit counter-example, we note the following identity that was obtained in the above proof together with an inequality in the sub-unital case that is a consequence of what we found so far.

## Lemma [label:lem:BDWSDPIimprovement]

Let $\matr_{d}(\CC)\xstoch{\mathcal{N}}\matr_{d'}(\CC)$ be a positive, trace-preserving map, and sub-unital map. Set $\rho:=\frac{1}{d}\mathds{1}_{d}$.
Then

$$

\relent{\sigma}{\rho}-\relent{\mathcal{N}(\sigma)}{\mathcal{N}(\rho)}=H\big(\N(\sigma)\big)-H(\sigma)+\tr\Big(\N(\sigma)\log\big(\N(\mathds{1}_{d})\big)\Big)

$$

and

$$

\relent{\sigma}{\rho}-\relent{\mathcal{N}(\sigma)}{\mathcal{N}(\rho)}-\relent{\sigma}{(\mathcal{R}^{\BDW}_{\rho,\N}\circ\mathcal{N})(\sigma)}\ge\tr\Big(\N(\sigma)\log\big(\N(\mathds{1}_{d})\big)\Big)

$$

for all density matrices $\sigma$ in $\matr_{d}(\CC)$. Here, $\mathcal{R}^{\BDW}_{\rho,\N}$ is the recovery map from Theorem~[ref:thm:BDWmain].

## Proof

The identity was obtained in the proof of Corollary~[ref:cor:BDWSDPI]. The inequality follows from this identity and Theorem~[ref:thm:BDWmain].

Lemma~[ref:lem:BDWSDPIimprovement] provides an improvement of the result from~[cite:BDW16] even though it is an immediate corollary. Note that the expression in the inequality from Lemma~[ref:lem:BDWSDPIimprovement] satisfies

$$

\tr\Big(\N(\sigma)\log\big(\N(\mathds{1}_{d})\big)\Big)\le0

$$

and is in particular not positive. This follows from the fact that this expression satisfies

$$
\tr\Big(\N(\sigma)\log\big(\N(\mathds{1}_{d})\big)\Big)&=\tr\Big(\N(\sigma)^{1/2}\log\big(\N(\mathds{1}_{d})\big)\N(\sigma)^{1/2}\Big)&&\text{by cyclicity of trace}\\
&\le\tr\big(\N(\sigma)^{1/2}\log(\mathds{1}_{d'})\N(\sigma)^{1/2}\big)&&\text{since $\N(\mathds{1}_{d})\le\mathds{1}_{d'}$}\\
&\le0&&\text{since $\log(\mathds{1}_{d'})\le0$.}
$$

Note that operator monotonicity of the logarithm was also used in the second line. This additional non-positive term prevents the result of~[cite:BDW16] from providing a strengthening of the DPI along the lines achieved in~[cite:FaRe15,Wilde15,JRSWW16,JRSWW18,SuToHa16]. Indeed, we illustrate this in the following explicit example.

## Example [label:ex:]

Let $\rho$ and $\N$ be as in Remark~[ref:rmk:CPTPSUBayesex].
We have already computed the Petz recovery map associated to these data. For reference, let us find the explicit form for the alternative recovery map of BDW

$$

\matr_{d'}(\CC)\ni B\xmapsto{\mathcal{R}^{\BDW}_{\rho,\N}} \mathcal{N}^*(B)+\Big(\tr(B)-\tr\big(\mathcal{N}^*(B)\big)\Big)\tau,

$$

where $\tau\in\matr_{d}(\CC)$ is some density matrix. Computing this on a some matrix $B\in\matr_{d'}(\CC)$ gives

$$

\R^{\BDW}_{\rho,\N}(B)=\frac{1-\epsilon}{d}\tr(B)\mathds{1}_{d}+\epsilon V^{\dag}BV+\epsilon\big(\tr(B)-\tr(V^{\dag}BV)\big)\tau.

$$

Notice that this is different from the Petz recovery map $\R^{P}_{\rho,\N}$ computed in Remark~[ref:rmk:CPTPSUBayesex] regardless of what density matrix $\tau$ is chosen. For simplicity, in the case that $\tau=\frac{\mathds{1}_{d}}{d},$ it becomes

$$

\R^{\BDW}_{\rho,\N}(B)=\frac{1}{d}\Big(\tr(B)-\epsilon\tr(V^{\dag}BV)\Big)\mathds{1}_{d}+\epsilon V^{\dag}BV.

$$

In order to compute the relevant relative entropy expressions, we note note that

$$

\log\big(\N(\mathds{1}_{d})\big)=\log\left(\frac{(1-\epsilon)d}{d'}\right)\mathds{1}_{d}+\log\left(\frac{(1-\epsilon)d+\epsilon d'}{(1-\epsilon)d}\right)VV^{\dag}.

$$

This together with Lemma~[ref:lem:BDWSDPIimprovement] gives an exact expression for the difference of relative entropies as

$$

\begin{split}
\relent{\sigma}{\rho}-\relent{\mathcal{N}(\sigma)}{\mathcal{N}(\rho)}

&=H\big(\N(\sigma)\big)-H(\sigma)+\log\left(\frac{(1-\epsilon)d}{d'}\right)\\

&+\left(\frac{(1-\epsilon)d+\epsilon d'}{d'}\right)\log\left(\frac{(1-\epsilon)d+\epsilon d'}{(1-\epsilon)d}\right)\\
\end{split}

$$

Let us now compare this to the expressions $\relent{\sigma}{(\R^{\BDW}_{\rho,\N}\circ\N)(\sigma)}$ and $\relent{\sigma}{(\R^{P}_{\rho,\N}\circ\N)(\sigma)}$ for arbitrary density matrices $\sigma\in\matr_{d'}(\CC)$. First, note that

$$

\N^*\big(\N(\sigma)\big)=(1-\epsilon)\left(\frac{1}{d'}+\frac{\epsilon}{d}\right)\mathds{1}_{d}+\epsilon^2 \sigma

$$

so that

$$

\R^{\BDW}_{\rho,\N}\big(\N(\sigma)\big)=\left(\frac{1-\epsilon^2}{d}\right)\mathds{1}_{d}+\epsilon^2\sigma.

$$

Spectrally decomposing $\sigma$ as $\sigma=\sum_{k}\lambda_{k}P_{k},$ where $\{P_{k}\}$ are orthogonal projections satisfying $\sum_{k}P_{k}=\mathds{1}_{d}$, gives

$$

\tr\left(\sigma\log\left(\R^{\BDW}_{\rho,\N}\big(\N(\sigma)\big)\right)\right)=\sum_{k}\lambda_{k}\tr(P_{k})\log\left(\frac{1-\epsilon^2}{d}+\epsilon^2\lambda_{k}\right)

$$

so that

$$

\relent{\sigma}{(\R^{\BDW}_{\rho,\N}\circ\N)(\sigma)}=-H(\sigma)-\sum_{k}\lambda_{k}\tr(P_{k})\log\left(\frac{1-\epsilon^2}{d}+\epsilon^2\lambda_{k}\right).

$$

Meanwhile,

$$

\R^{P}_{\rho,\N}\big(\N(\sigma)\big)=

\left(\frac{(1-\epsilon)d'}{d^2}+\frac{\epsilon(1-\epsilon)}{(1-\epsilon)d+\epsilon d'}\right)\mathds{1}_{d}
+\left(\frac{\epsilon^2 d'}{(1-\epsilon)d+\epsilon d'}\right)\sigma

$$

so that

$$

\relent{\sigma}{(\R^{P}_{\rho,\N}\circ\N)(\sigma)}=-H(\sigma)-\sum_{k}\lambda_{k}\tr(P_{k})\log\left(\frac{(1-\epsilon)d'}{d^2}+\frac{\epsilon(1-\epsilon)+\epsilon^2 d'\lambda_{k}}{(1-\epsilon)d+\epsilon d'}\right).

$$

As for the entropy of $\N(\sigma)$, note that $\{V P_{k}V^{\dag}\}$ together with $\mathds{1}_{d'}-VV^{\dag}$ provide a spectral decomposition of $\N(\sigma)$ since $V$ is an isometry. The spectral decomposition is given explicitly by

$$

\N(\sigma)=\sum_{k}\left(\frac{1-\epsilon}{d'}+\epsilon\lambda_{k}\right)VP_{k}V^{\dag}+\frac{1-\epsilon}{d'}\left(\mathds{1}_{d'}-VV^{\dag}\right).

$$

Therefore, the associated entropy is

$$

H\big(\N(\sigma)\big)=-\sum_{k}\left(\frac{1-\epsilon}{d'}+\epsilon\lambda_{k}\right)\tr(P_{k})\log\left(\frac{1-\epsilon}{d'}+\epsilon\lambda_{k}\right)-\frac{(1-\epsilon)(d'-d)}{d'}\log\left(\frac{1-\epsilon}{d'}\right)

$$

since $\tr(\mathds{1}_{d'}-VV^{\dag})=d'-d$. With this, we get

$$

\begin{split}
SDPI[\sigma,\rho,\mathcal{N},\mathcal{R}^{\BDW}_{\rho,\N}]

&=\sum_{k}\tr(P_{k})\lambda_{k}\log\left(\frac{1-\epsilon^2}{d}+\epsilon^2\lambda_{k}\right)\\
&-\sum_{k}\tr(P_{k})\left(\frac{1-\epsilon}{d'}+\epsilon\lambda_{k}\right)\log\left(\frac{1-\epsilon}{d'}+\epsilon\lambda_{k}\right)

+\log(d)+\Delta\log(\Delta)
\end{split}

$$

and

$$

\begin{split}
SDPI[\sigma,\rho,\mathcal{N},\mathcal{R}^{P}_{\rho,\N}]&=

\sum_{k}\tr(P_{k})\lambda_{k}\log\left(\frac{1-\epsilon^2}{\Delta d}+\frac{(1-\epsilon)\epsilon(1-r)^2}{\Delta d'}+\frac{\epsilon^2 \lambda_{k}}{\Delta}\right)\\
&-\sum_{k}\tr(P_{k})\left(\frac{1-\epsilon}{d'}+\epsilon\lambda_{k}\right)\log\left(\frac{1-\epsilon}{d'}+\epsilon\lambda_{k}\right)

+\log(d)+\Delta\log(\Delta),
\end{split}

$$

where we have introduced the notation

$$

\Delta:=\frac{(1-\epsilon)d+\epsilon d'}{d'}
\qquad\text{ and }\qquad
r:=\frac{d'}{d}.

$$

Note that both of these expressions only depend on the eigenvalues of $\sigma$, the dimensions $d$ and $d'$, and the parameter $\epsilon$. As such, in the case where $d=2$ and $d'=3$, we can parametrize the eigenvalues of $\sigma$ by a single parameter $\lambda\in[0,1]$ and then use the remaining parameter $\epsilon$ to plot these expressions. This is done in Figure~ .

This motivates the question: What sufficient conditions for sub-unital maps guarantees that the strengthened DPI holds? The following result illustrates the importance of Bayesian invertibility in answering this question.

## Theorem [label:thm:CPTPSUBayesSDPI]

Let $d,d'\in\NN$ and
let $\A:=\matr_{d}(\CC)\xstoch{\mathcal{N}}\matr_{d'}(\CC)=:\B$ be a postive, trace-preserving, and sub-unital map. Set $\omega=\frac{1}{d}\tr$, $\rho:=\frac{1}{d}\mathds{1}_{d}$, and $F:=\mathcal{N}^*$, the Hilbert--Schmidt dual of $F$. If $(F,\omega)$ is Bayesian invertible, then

$$

\relent{\sigma}{\rho}-\relent{\mathcal{N}(\sigma)}{\mathcal{N}(\rho)}-\relent{\sigma}{(\mathcal{P}\circ\mathcal{N})(\sigma)}\ge0

$$

for all density matrices $\sigma$ in $\matr_{d}(\CC)$. Here, $\mathcal{P}$ is the Hilbert--Schmidt dual of a Bayesian inverse to $(F,\omega)$ ($\mathcal{P}$ equals the Petz recovery map when $\mathcal{N}(\rho)$ is invertible).

## Proof

By Proposition~5.12 item~ii in~[cite:PaRuBayes] and Lemma~[ref:lem:imageofchannel], the pair $(F,\omega)$ is Bayesian invertible if and only if $[\mathcal{N}(A),\mathcal{N}(\mathds{1}_{d})]=0$ for all $A\in\A$. By the non-commutative Bayes' theorem for matrix algebras~[cite:PaRuBayes], the form of a Bayesian inverse to $(F,\omega)$ is given by

$$

\A\ni A\mapsto G(A):=\widehat{\mathcal{N}(\mathds{1}_{d})}^{1/2}\mathcal{N}(A)\widehat{\mathcal{N}(\mathds{1}_{d})}^{1/2}+\zeta(A)P^{\perp}

$$

for some state $\zeta=\tr(\tau\;\cdot\;)$ on $A$. Here, $P$ is the support projection associated to $\mathcal{N}(\mathds{1}_{d})$.
Hence, the Hilbert--Schmidt dual is

$$

\mathcal{P}(B):=G^*(B)
=\mathcal{N}^*\left(\widehat{\mathcal{N}(\mathds{1}_{d})}^{1/2}B\widehat{\mathcal{N}(\mathds{1}_{d})}^{1/2}\right)+\tr(P^{\perp} B)\tau
\equiv\mathcal{P}_{\rho,\mathcal{N}}(B)+\tr(P^{\perp} B)\tau.

$$

From this, we obtain

$$

\begin{split}
SDPI&[\sigma,\rho,\mathcal{N},\mathcal{P}]
=H\big(\mathcal{N}(\sigma)\big)-H(\sigma)+\tr\Big(\mathcal{N}(\sigma)\ln\big(\mathcal{N}(\mathds{1}_{d})\big)\Big)-\relent{\sigma}{(\mathcal{P}\circ\mathcal{N})(\sigma)}\\
&\ge H\big(\mathcal{N}(\sigma)\big)-H(\sigma)+\tr\Big(\mathcal{N}(\sigma)\ln\big(\mathcal{N}(\mathds{1}_{d})\big)\Big)-\relent{\sigma}{(\mathcal{P}_{\rho,\mathcal{N}}\circ\mathcal{N})(\sigma)}\\
&=H\big(\mathcal{N}(\sigma)\big)+\tr\Big(\mathcal{N}(\sigma)\ln\big(\mathcal{N}(\mathds{1}_{d})\big)\Big)+\tr\bigg(\sigma\ln\Big(\mathcal{N}^*\big(\widehat{\mathcal{N}(\mathds{1}_{d})}^{1/2}\mathcal{N}(\sigma)\widehat{\mathcal{N}(\mathds{1}_{d})}^{1/2}\big)\Big)\bigg)\\
&\ge H\big(\mathcal{N}(\sigma)\big)+\tr\Big(\mathcal{N}(\sigma)\ln\big(\mathcal{N}(\mathds{1}_{d})\big)\Big)+\tr\bigg(\sigma\mathcal{N}^*\Big(\ln\big(\widehat{\mathcal{N}(\mathds{1}_{d})}^{1/2}\mathcal{N}(\sigma)\widehat{\mathcal{N}(\mathds{1}_{d})}^{1/2}\big)\Big)\bigg)\\

&=H\big(\mathcal{N}(\sigma)\big)+\tr\Big(\mathcal{N}(\sigma)\ln\big(\mathcal{N}(\mathds{1}_{d})\big)\Big)+\tr\Big(\mathcal{N}(\sigma)\ln\big(\widehat{\mathcal{N}(\mathds{1}_{d})}\big)+\mathcal{N}(\sigma)\ln\big(\mathcal{N}(\sigma)\big)\Big)\\
&=0.
\end{split}

$$

The second inequality follows from a property of the relative entropy (see Equation (11) in~[cite:BDW16] for example).
The second inequality follows from the Choi--Davis--Jensen inequality, which applies to $\mathcal{N}^*$ since $\mathcal{N}$ is CPTP.
The fifth line follows from the definition of the Hilbert--Schmidt adjoint and also the Bayes' condition since $\mathcal{N}(\mathds{1}_{d})$ commutes with $\mathcal{N}(\sigma)$. By the functional calculus, $\widehat{\mathcal{N}(\mathds{1}_{d})}^{1/2}$ commutes with $\mathcal{N}(\sigma)$, which implies that the logarithm of a product can be split into the corresponding sum of logarithms.

## Remark

The map $\mathcal{N}$ from Remark~[ref:rmk:CPTPSUBayesex] satisfies the assumptions of Theorem~[ref:thm:CPTPSUBayesSDPI], namely $(F,\omega)$ is Bayesian invertible, where $F=\N^*$ and $\omega=\frac{1}{d}\tr$. However, it should be pointed out that the recovery map $\mathcal{R}$ from Theorem~[ref:thm:BDWmain] does not in general satisfy the SDPI. Therefore, we obtain an even stronger DPI by using the Bayesian inverse instead of the recovery map of Buscemi, Das, and Wilde~[cite:BDW16].

The assumption of Bayesian invertibility in Theorem~[ref:thm:CPTPSUBayesSDPI] is not automatic as the following example illustrates.

## Example

Given $\epsilon,\delta\in(0,1)$ and two isometries $V,W:\CC^{d}\to\CC^{d'}$ such that $[VV^{\dag},WW^{\dag}]\ne0$, set

$$

\A\ni A\mapsto\mathcal{N}(A):=\frac{1-\epsilon-\delta}{d'}\tr(A)\mathds{1}_{d'}+\epsilon VAV^{\dag}+\delta WAW^{\dag}.

$$

Also, set $\rho:=\frac{1}{d}\mathds{1}_{d}$ and $\omega:=\tr(\rho\;\cdot\;)$.
Then the pair $(F:=\mathcal{N}^*,\omega)$ is not Bayesian invertible.

### Thermal operations are Bayesian invertibile

In~[cite:AWWW18], the SDPI was proven for thermal operations. In fact, more general conditions were found under which the SDPI holds. In the following proposition, we show that the most general operations considered in~[cite:AWWW18] for which the SDPI holds are Bayesian invertible.

## Proposition

Let $\H$ be a Hilbert space, $\rho$ a full-rank density matrix on $\H$, and set $\A:=\B(\H)$. Let $\A\xstoch{\Phi}\A$ be a quantum channel for which $\rho$ is fixed, i.e., $\Phi(\rho)=\rho$, and with a dilation of the form

$$

\xy0;/r.25pc/:
(-12.5,-7.5)*+{\A}="in";
(-12.5,7.5)*+{\A\otimes\B}="tot";
(12.5,7.5)*+{\A\otimes\B}="tot2";
(12.5,-7.5)*+{\A}="out";
{\ar@{~>}"in";"tot"^{\id\otimes\tau}};
{\ar"tot";"tot2"^{\Ad_{U}}};
{\ar"tot2";"out"^{\Tr_{\B}}};
{\ar@{~>}"in";"out"_{\Phi}};
\endxy

$$

for some $\B:=\B(\K)$ with $\K$ a Hilbert space, $\tau$ a density matrix on $\K$, and $U\in\A\otimes\B$ a unitary on $\H\otimes\K$. In addition, suppose that there exists a density matrix $\tau'\in\B$ such that

$$

U(\rho\otimes\tau)U^{\dag}=\rho\otimes\tau'.

$$

Then the pair $(F,\omega)$, where $F:=\Phi^*$ and $\omega=\tr(\rho\;\cdot\;)$, is Bayesian invertible. Furthermore, the Bayesian inverse of $(F,\omega)$ is given by the Hilbert--Schmidt dual of the Petz recovery map $\mathcal{R}$, which is given by

$$

\xy0;/r.25pc/:
(-12.5,-7.5)*+{\A}="in";
(-12.5,7.5)*+{\A\otimes\B}="tot";
(12.5,7.5)*+{\A\otimes\B}="tot2";
(12.5,-7.5)*+{\A}="out";
{\ar"tot";"in"_{\Tr_{\B}}};
{\ar"tot2";"tot"_{\Ad_{U^{\dag}}}};
{\ar@{~>}"out";"tot2"_{\id\otimes\tau'}};
{\ar@{~>}"out";"in"^{\mathcal{R}}};
\endxy
\;\;.

$$

## Proof

By~[cite:PaRuBayes] and the fact that $\Phi(\rho)=\rho$ is a full-rank density matrix, it suffices to check $\Phi(\rho A)\rho=\rho\Phi(A\rho)$ for all $A\in\A$. This follows from the calculation

$$

\begin{split}
\Phi(\rho A)\rho&=\Tr_{\B}\big(U(\rho A\otimes\tau)U^{\dag}\big)\rho\\
&=\Tr_{\B}\big(U(\rho\otimes\tau)U^{\dag}U(A\otimes1_{\B})U^{\dag}(\rho\otimes1_{\B})\big)\\
&=\Tr_{\B}\big((\rho\otimes\tau')U(A\otimes1_{\B})U^{\dag}(\rho\otimes1_{\B})\big)\\
&=\rho\Tr_{\B}\big((1_{\A}\otimes\tau')U(A\otimes1_{\B})U^{\dag}(\rho\otimes1_{\B})\big)\\
&=\rho\Tr_{\B}\big(U(A\otimes1_{\B})U^{\dag}(\rho\otimes\tau')UU^{\dag}\big)\\
&=\rho\Tr_{\B}\big(U(A\otimes1_{\B})(\rho\otimes\tau')U^{\dag}\big)\\
&=\rho\Tr_{\B}\big(U(A\rho\otimes\tau)U^{\dag}\big)\\
&=\rho\Phi(A\rho).
\qedhere
\end{split}

$$

Examples of such quantum channels are thermal operations and more generally isentropic catalytic thermal operations (see~[cite:AWWW18] for more details).

### Davies maps are Bayesian invertible with respect to the Gibbs state

Davies maps are occasionally used to describe Markovian evolution for systems in contact with a heat bath~[cite:RFZ10]. It has recently been shown that Davies maps satisfy the SDPI in~[cite:AlWo17]. In the following, $[\;\cdot\;,\;\cdot\;]$ and $\{\;\cdot\;,\;\cdot\;\}$ denote the commutator and anti-commutator, respectively.

## Definition [label:defn:Daviesmap]

A CPTP map $\matr_{m}(\CC)\xstoch{\Phi}\matr_{m}(\CC)$ is called a if there exist

[(a)]

-
a self-adjoint operator $H$, called a Hamiltonian.

-
a Lindblad operator $\mathcal{L}$ described by Kraus operators via

$$

\matr_{m}(\CC)\ni\rho\xmapsto{\mathcal{L}}\sum_{\alpha}\left(K_{\alpha}\rho K_{\alpha}^{\dag}-\frac{1}{2}\left\{K_{\alpha}^{\dag}K_{\alpha},\rho\right\}\right),

$$

-
and a time $t\in\RR_{\ge 0}$

such that

-
$\Phi=e^{t\mathcal{G}},$ where $\mathcal{G}=i\delta+\mathcal{L}$ with $\delta$ the derivation given by $\delta:=[H,\;\cdot\;]$,

-
$\delta$ and $\mathcal{L}$ commute, and

-
$\mathcal{L}$ satisfies

$$

\tr\big(\mathcal{L}(B\rho_{\beta})A\big)=\tr\big(\mathcal{L}(\rho_{\beta}A)B\big)
\qquad\forall\;A,\,B\in\matr_{m}(\CC),

$$

where $\rho_{\beta}$ is the Gibbs density associated to $H$

$$

\rho_{\beta}:=\frac{1}{\mathcal{Z}}e^{-\beta H}, \qquad\mathcal{Z}:=\tr\left(e^{-\beta H}\right)

$$

with respect to inverse temperature $\beta$.

## Lemma [label:lem:Daviesproperties]

Let $\Phi$ be a Davies map as in Definition~[ref:defn:Daviesmap]. Then the following facts hold.

[(a)]

-
$\Phi=e^{t\mathcal{L}}\circ\Ad_{e^{it H}}$.

-
$e^{i\delta}$, $e^{t\mathcal{L}}$, and $\Phi$ are all $\dag$-preserving.

-
$\Phi^*=e^{t(-i\delta+\mathcal{L}^*)}\equiv e^{t\mathcal{L}^*}\circ\Ad_{e^{-it H}}$.

-
$\mathcal{L}^*$ is given by

$$

\matr_{m}(\CC)\ni A\xmapsto{\mathcal{L}^*}\sum_{\alpha}
\left(K_{\alpha}^{\dag}A K_{\alpha}-\frac{1}{2}\left\{K_{\alpha}^{\dag}K_{\alpha},A\right\}\right).

$$

-
$\tr\circ\mathcal{L}=0$.

-
$\mathcal{L}(\rho_{\beta})=0$.

-
$\Phi(\rho_{\beta})=\rho_{\beta}$.

## Proof

you found me!

[(a)]

-
Since $\delta$ and $\mathcal{L}$ commute, it immediately follows that $\Phi=e^{t\mathcal{L}}\circ e^{t i\delta}$. Hence, it suffices to show $e^{t i\delta}=\Ad_{e^{it H}}$. This is a simple exercise in Taylor expansion.

-
Since we know $e^{t i\delta}=\Ad_{e^{it H}}$ is $\dag$-preserving, it suffices to prove $e^{t\mathcal{L}}$ is $\dag$-preserving. This follows from a direct calculation that shows $\mathcal{L}(\rho^{\dag})^{\dag}=\mathcal{L}(\rho)$ for all $\rho\in\matr_{m}(\CC)$.

-
By the commutativity assumptions and the involutive property of the Hilbert--Schmidt adjoint, it suffices to prove $(e^{t\mathcal{L}})^{*}=e^{t\mathcal{L}^*}$.

-
This follows from the fact that the Hilbert--Schmidt dual of $Ad_{V}$ is $Ad_{V^{\dag}}$ and that of $\rho\mapsto\{Q,\rho\}$ is $A\mapsto\{Q,A\}$ whenever $Q$ is positive.

-
This follows immediately from the cyclicity property of the trace.

-
Since $\mathcal{L}$ satisfies $\tr\big(\mathcal{L}(B\rho_{\beta})A\big)=\tr\big(\mathcal{L}(\rho_{\beta}A)B\big)$ for all $A,\,B\in\matr_{m}(\CC)$, taking $A=\mathds{1}_{m}$ gives $\tr\big(\mathcal{L}(B\rho_{\beta})\big)=\tr\big(\mathcal{L}(\rho_{\beta})B\big)$ for all $B\in\matr_{m}(\CC)$. But the left-hand-side of this expression is $(\tr\circ\mathcal{L})(B\rho_{\beta})=0$. This implies $\mathcal{L}(\rho_{\beta})=0$.

-
Since $e^{ti\delta}(\rho_{\beta})=Ad_{e^{it H}}(\rho_{\beta})=\rho_{\beta}$, it suffices to show $e^{t\mathcal{L}}(\rho_{\beta})=\rho_{\beta}$. But this follows immediately by Taylor expanding and the fact that $\mathcal{L}(\rho_{\beta})=0$.

## Lemma [label:lem:Daviesbinary]

Let $\matr_{m}(\CC)\xstoch{\Psi}\matr_{m}(\CC)$ be any $\dag$-preserving map and let $\rho$ be an invertible density matrix. Then the following conditions are equivalent.

[i.]

-

$\omega\big(A\Psi^{*}(B)\big)=\omega\big(\Psi^*(A)B\big)$ for all $A,\,B\in\matr_{m}(\CC)$, where $\omega=\tr(\rho\;\cdot\;)$.

-

$\tr\big(\rho A^{\dag}\Psi^{*}(B)\big)=\tr\big(\rho\Psi^*(A)^{\dag}B\big)$ for all $A,\,B\in\matr_{m}(\CC)$.

-

$\tr\big(\Psi(B\rho)A\big)=\tr\big(\Psi(\rho A)B\big)$ for all $A,\,B\in\matr_{m}(\CC)$.

-

$\tr\big(\rho^{-1}X^{\dag}\Psi(Y)\big)=\tr\big(\rho^{-1}\Psi(X)^{\dag}Y\big)$ for all $X,\,Y\in\matr_{m}(\CC)$.

## Proof

you found me!

($[ref:item:DaviesBayesexp]\Leftrightarrow[ref:item:DaviesBayes]$)
This follows from the fact that $\dag$ is an involution and $\Psi^*$ is $\dag$-preserving since $\Psi$ is.

($[ref:item:DaviesBayes]\Leftrightarrow[ref:item:DaviesQDB]$) Item~$[ref:item:DaviesBayes]$ is equivalent to
$\tr\big((A\rho)^{\dag}\Psi^{*}(B)\big)=\tr\big(\Psi^*(A)^{\dag}B\rho\big)$ for all $A,\,B\in\matr_{m}(\CC)$. By using the definition of the Hilbert--Schmidt adjoint, this is equivalent to
$\tr\big(\Psi(A\rho)^{\dag}B\big)=\tr\big(A^{\dag}\Psi(B\rho)\big)$ for all $A,\,B\in\matr_{m}(\CC)$.
Since $\Psi$ is $\dag$-preserving, this is equivalent to
$\tr\big(\Psi(\rho A^{\dag})B\big)=\tr\big(A^{\dag}\Psi(B\rho)\big)$ for all $A,\,B\in\matr_{m}(\CC)$. Finally, since $\dag$ is an involution, this is equivalent to item~$[ref:item:DaviesQDB]$.

($[ref:item:DaviesQDB]\Rightarrow[ref:item:DaviesAltQDB]$) Since right and left multiplication by $\rho^{-1}$ are linear isomorphisms, taking $B=Y\rho^{-1}$ and $A=\rho^{-1}X^{\dag}$ gives $\tr\big(\Psi(Y)\rho^{-1}X^{\dag}\big)=\tr\big(\Psi(X^{\dag})Y\rho^{-1}\big)$ for all $X,\,Y\in\matr_{m}(\CC)$. Since $\Psi$ is $\dag$-preserving, this gives item~[ref:item:DaviesAltQDB].

($[ref:item:DaviesQDB]\Leftarrow[ref:item:DaviesAltQDB]$) This direction is obtained along similar lines to its converse by taking $X=A^{\dag}\rho$ and $Y=B\rho$.

## Lemma [label:lem:DaviesmapssatisfiesQDB]

Let $\Phi=e^{t(i\delta+\mathcal{L})}$ be a Davies map as in Definition~[ref:defn:Daviesmap] with Gibbs density matrix $\rho_{\beta}$ and associated Gibbs state $\omega=\tr(\rho_{\beta}\;\cdot\;)$.
Then

$$

\left\langle X,e^{ti\delta}(Y)\right\rangle_{\beta}=\left\langle e^{-ti\delta}(X),Y\right\rangle_{\beta}
\quad\text{ and }\quad

\left\langle X,e^{t\mathcal{L}}(Y)\right\rangle_{\beta}=\left\langle e^{t\mathcal{L}}(X),Y\right\rangle_{\beta}
\quad\forall\;X,\,Y\in\matr_{m}(\CC),

$$

where $\langle A,B\rangle_{\beta}:=\tr(\rho_{\beta}^{-1}A^{\dag}B)$. In particular,

$$

\left\langle X, e^{t(i\delta+\mathcal{L})}(Y)\right\rangle_{\beta}=\left\langle e^{t(-i\delta+\mathcal{L})}(X),Y\right\rangle_{\beta}
\qquad\forall\;X,\,Y\in\matr_{m}(\CC).

$$

## Proof

The second claim follows from the first two because of the commuting conditions for $\delta$ and $\mathcal{L}$ as well as the compositional property of adjoints since $\Phi=e^{t\mathcal{L}}\circ Ad_{e^{itH}}$.
It therefore suffices to prove $\left\langle X,Ad_{e^{itH}}(Y)\right\rangle_{\beta}=\left\langleAd_{e^{-itH}}(X),Y\right\rangle_{\beta}$ and $\left\langle X,e^{t\mathcal{L}}(Y)\right\rangle_{\beta}=\left\langle e^{t\mathcal{L}}(X),Y\right\rangle_{\beta}$.
The first claim follows from a simple calculation using cyclicity of the trace and the fact that $[H,\rho_{\beta}]=0$.
The second claim follows from the fact that the identity $\left\langle X,\mathcal{L}(Y)\right\rangle_{\beta}=\left\langle\mathcal{L}(X),Y\right\rangle_{\beta}$ holds by Lemma~[ref:lem:Daviesproperties] and Lemma~[ref:lem:Daviesbinary].

## Theorem

Let $\Phi=e^{t(i\delta+\mathcal{L})}$ be a Davies map as in Definition~[ref:defn:Daviesmap] with Gibbs density matrix $\rho_{\beta}$ and associated Gibbs state $\omega=\tr(\rho_{\beta}\;\cdot\;)$. Set $F:=\Phi^*\equiv e^{t(-i\delta+\mathcal{L}^{*})}$. Then $G:=e^{t(i\delta+\mathcal{L}^*)}$ is a Bayesian inverse of $(F,\omega)$.

## Proof

Since $F=e^{t\mathcal{L}^{*}}\circAd_{e^{-itH}}$ and each component fixes the Gibbs state, i.e., $\omega\circ e^{t\mathcal{L}^{*}}=\omega$ and $\omega\circAd_{e^{-itH}}$, by the compositional property of Bayesian inverses, it suffices to prove that $Ad_{e^{itH}}$ and $e^{t\mathcal{L}^*}$ are Bayesian inverses of $(Ad_{e^{-itH}},\omega)$ and $(e^{t\mathcal{L}^*},\omega)$ respectively. The first claim is immediate because $Ad_{e^{itH}}$ is a $*$-isomorphism that fixes $\omega$. Meanwhile, the second claim follows from Lemma~[ref:lem:DaviesmapssatisfiesQDB] and Lemma~[ref:lem:Daviesbinary]. Thus, $\omega\big(AF(B)\big)=\omega\big(G(A)B\big)$, which is precisely the Bayes condition because $\omega=\omega\circ F$.

### Bayesian invertibility of approximate broadcasting and symmetric subspaces

In~[cite:LeWi17], Lemm and Wilde proved a strengthened data-processing inequality in terms of maximally mixed states on symmetric subspaces undergoing a symmetric partial trace operation. The recovery map is a symmetric broadcasting channel.
To precisely state their result and relate it to our framework of Bayesian inversion, we first recall the necessary definitions~[cite:Ha13].

Fix natural numbers $d$ and $n$. Let $\H=(\CC^{d})^{\otimes n}$. If $V$ is a vector space, then the permutation group $S_{n}$ on $n$ distinct elements, which are taken to be $\{1,\dots,n\}$, acts on $V^{\otimes n}$ by sending $\sigma\in S_{n}$ to the linear isomorphism $P_{V}(\sigma):V^{\otimes n}\to V^{\otimes n}$ uniquely determined on product tensors by

$$

V^{\otimes n}\ni v_{1}\otimes\cdots\otimes v_{n}\mapsto v_{\sigma(1)}\otimes\cdots\otimes v_{\sigma(n)}.

$$

When $V=\CC^{d}$, this representation is often denoted by $P_{d}$.
The of $V^{\otimes n}$ is given by

$$

V^{\otimes n}_{sym}
:=
\left\{v\in V^{\otimes n} \;:\; P(\sigma)v=v\quad\forall\;\sigma\in S_{n}\right\}.

$$

Note that if $d$ is the dimension of $V$, then

$$

dim(V^{\otimes n}_{sym})=\frac{d(d+1)\cdots(d+n-1)}{n!}=:d[n].

$$

Let $\Pi^{d,n}_{sym}$ denote the orthogonal projection from $\H$ onto the symmetric subspace $\H_{sym}$.
Explicitly,

$$

\Pi^{d,n}_{sym}=\frac{1}{n!}\sum_{\sigma\in S_{n}}P(\sigma).

$$

Let

$$

\pi^{d,n}_{sym}=\frac{1}{d[n]}\Pi^{d,n}_{sym}

$$

be the maximally mixed density matrix supported on this symmetric subspace.
Now, let $k\le n$ be another natural number and set $\K=(\CC^{d})^{\otimes k}$. Also, set $\A:=\mathcal{B}(\H)$ and $\B:=\mathcal{B}(\K)$.
Let $\B\xleftarrow{\tr_{k\leftarrow n}}\A$ denote the partial trace uniquely determined by

$$

\A\ni A_{1}\otimes\cdots\otimes A_{n}\mapsto\tr(A_{1})\cdots\tr(A_{n-k})A_{n-k+1}\otimes\cdots\otimes A_{n}\in\B.

$$

Let $\B\xleftarrow{\mathcal{P}_{k\leftarrow n}}\A$ denote the , which is given by

$$

\mathcal{P}_{k\leftarrow n}=\Ad_{\Pi^{d,k}_{sym}}\circ\tr_{k\leftarrow n}\circ\Ad_{\Pi^{d,n}_{sym}}.

$$

The associated to this symmetrized partial trace is given by

$$

\K_{sym}\ni\tau\mapsto\mathcal{C}_{n\leftarrow k}(\tau):=\frac{d[k]}{d[n]}\Pi^{d,n}_{sym}\Big(\big(\Pi^{d,k}_{sym}\tau\Pi^{d,k}_{sym}\big)\otimes\mathds{1}_{d}^{\otimes(n-k)}\Big)\Pi^{d,n}_{sym}\in\H_{sym}.

$$

The two maps satisfy the following properties

$$

\mathcal{P}_{k\leftarrow n}^{*}=\left(\frac{d[n]}{d[k]}\right)\mathcal{C}_{n\leftarrow{k}},
\qquad
\mathcal{P}_{k\leftarrow n}\left(\pi^{d,n}_{sym}\right)=\pi^{d,k}_{sym},
\quad\text{ and }\quad
\mathcal{C}_{n\leftarrow{k}}\left(\pi^{d,k}_{sym}\right)=\pi^{d,n}_{sym}.

$$

## Theorem

Using the notation introduced in this subsection, set $F:=\mathcal{P}_{k\leftarrow n}^{*}$ and $\omega:=\tr(\pi^{d,n}_{sym}\;\cdot\;)$. Then $G:=\mathcal{C}_{n\leftarrow k}^{*}$ is a Bayesian inverse of $(F,\omega)$.

## Proof

### Conditional mutual information

In what follows, let $\Hom^{+}(\B,\A)$ denote the convex space of positive maps from a $C^*$-algebra $\B$ to another one $\A$.

## Definition [label:defn:recoverymapprocedure]

A (in the Heisenberg picture) is an assignment sending every pair of finite-dimensional $C^*$-algebras $\A$ and $\B$ to a function

$$

\begin{split}
\Hom^{+}(\A,\CC)\times\Hom^{+}(\B,\A)&\xrightarrow{\mathcal{T}}\Hom^{+}(\A,\B)\\
(\omega,F)&\mapsto \mathcal{T}_{\omega,F}
\end{split}

$$

satisfying the following properties

-

$\mathcal{T}_{\omega,F\circ G}\aeequals{\omega\circ F\circ G}\mathcal{T}_{\omega\circ F,G}\circ\mathcal{T}_{\omega,F}$ for all $\omega\in\Hom^{+}(\A,\CC)$, $F\in\Hom^{+}(\B,\A)$, and $G\in\Hom^{+}(\C,\B)$ (a.e.\ compositionality)

-

$\mathcal{T}_{\omega,\id_{\A}}\aeequals{\omega}\id_{\A}$ for all $\omega\in\Hom^{+}(\A,\CC)$ (a.e.\ unitality)

-
$\mathcal{T}_{\omega\otimes\xi,F\otimes G}\aeequals{(\omega\circ F)\otimes(\xi\circ G)}\mathcal{T}_{\omega,F}\otimes\mathcal{T}_{\xi,F}$ for all $\omega\in\Hom^{+}(\A,\CC)$, $\xi\in\Hom^{+}(\C,\CC)$, $F\in\Hom^{+}(\B,\A)$, and $G\in\Hom^{+}(\D,\C)$ (a.e.\ tensoriality)

-
$\omega\circ F\circ\mathcal{T}_{\omega,F}=\omega$ for all $\omega\in\Hom^{+}(\A,\CC)$ and $F\in\Hom^{+}(\B,\A)$ (state-preservation)

-

$\mathcal{T}_{\omega,F}\aeequals{\omega\circ F}F^{-1}$ for all $\omega\in\Hom^{+}(\A,\CC)$ and for all $*$-isomorphisms $F\in\Hom^{+}(\B,\A)$.

-

$\mathcal{T}_{\omega,F}$ is unital whenever $F$ is unital and $\omega$ is a state.

The notation

$$

\begin{split}
\A^{+}\times\Hom^{+}(\A,\B)&\xrightarrow{\mathcal{R}}\Hom^{+}(\B,\A)\\
(\rho,\N)&\mapsto \mathcal{R}_{\rho,\N}
\end{split}

$$

will be used for the analogous recovery map procedure in the Schr\"odinger picture.

Some of these properties of a good recovery map were isolated in~[cite:Wilde15]. There are some subtleties when the states are not faithful, but we will not concern ourselves with that for the time being.

## Proposition

When restricted to faithful states and positive trace-preserving maps, the Petz recovery map is defines a recovery map procedure. Furthermore, it takes CPU maps to CPU maps when the input and output states are faithful.

## Remark

The Petz recovery map fails to satisfy properties~[ref:item:recoveryidentity], [ref:item:recoveryinverse], and~[ref:item:recoveryunital] in Definition~[ref:defn:recoverymapprocedure] when the states are not faithful. However, the other properties remain valid. Proofs of these claims are given in~[cite:Wilde15], with the exception of the proof of item~[ref:item:recoverycompositionality] (which was only proven in~[cite:Wilde15] in the faithful case). As such, we include the proof here.

Now, let $\rho:=\rho_{\A\E\B}$ be a density matrix on $\A\otimes\E\otimes\B$. Set $\sigma:=\rho_{\A}\otimes\rho_{\E\B}$, where $\rho_{\A}=\Tr_{\B\E}(\rho)$ and $\rho_{\E\B}=\Tr_{\A}(\rho)$. Let $\N:\A\otimes\E\otimes\B\to\A\otimes\E$ be the partial trace over $\B$, i.e., $\N:=\Tr_{\B}$. Then

$$

\begin{split}
\relent{\rho}{\sigma}-\relent{\N(\rho)}{\N(\sigma)}&=\relent{\rho_{\A\E\B}}{\rho_{\A}\otimes\rho_{\E\B}}-\relent{\Tr_{\B}(\rho_{\A\E\B})}{\Tr_{\B}(\rho_{\A}\otimes\rho_{\E\B})}\\
&=\relent{\rho_{\A\E\B}}{\rho_{\A}\otimes\rho_{\E\B}}-\relent{\rho_{\A\E}}{\rho_{\A}\otimes\rho_{\E}}\\
&=I(\A:\B|\E)_{\rho},
\end{split}

$$

where

$$

I(\A:\B|\E)_{\rho}:=S(\rho_{\A\E})+S(\rho_{\E\B})-S(\rho_{\E})-S(\rho_{\A\E\B})

$$

denotes the conditional mutual information of $\A$ and $\B$ given $\E$~[cite:LiWi18]. Let us assume that $\rho$ has full rank. Then, by the definition of a recovery map procedure,

$$

\R_{\sigma,\N}
=\R_{\rho_{\A},\id_{\A}}\otimes\R_{\rho_{\E\B},\Tr_{\B}}
=\id_{\A}\otimes\widehat{\R},

$$

where $\widehat{\R}:=\R_{\rho_{\E\B},\Tr_{\B}}:\E\to\E\otimes\B$ and we have slightly abused notation here since the partial trace is of the form $\Tr_{\B}:\E\otimes\B\to\E$. Therefore, the SDPI in this case takes the form

$$

I(\A:\B|\E)_{\rho}-\relent{\rho_{\A\E\B}}{(\id_{\A}\otimes\widehat{R})(\rho_{\A\E})}\ge0.

$$

### Covariant channels

## Definition [label:defn:stateunitaries]

Let $\rho\in\matr_{m}(\CC)$ be a density matrix and let $\rho=\sum_{k=1}^{m}p_{k}P_{k}$ be an orthonormal decomposition of $\rho$.
From these data, define the smooth map

$$

\begin{split}
\mathbb{T}^{m}&\xrightarrow{U_{\rho}}\mathcal{U}(m)\\
\vartheta\equiv(\vartheta_{1},\dots,\vartheta_{m})&\xmapsto{\phantom{xx}} U^{\vartheta}_{\rho}:=\sum_{k}e^{i\vartheta_{k}}P_{k},
\end{split}

$$

where $\mathbb{T}^{m}:=\mathcal{U}(1)\times\cdots\times \mathcal{U}(1)$ is the $m$-torus, viewed as the quotient of $[0,2\pi]^{m}$ under the standard identifications, and $\mathcal{U}(m)$ is the group of unitary $m\times m$ matrices.

## Definition [label:defn:covarianceandrotatedPetz]

Let $\A=\matr_{m}(\CC)$ and $\B=\matr_{n}(\CC)$ be matrix algebras, let $\alpha=\tr(\rho\;\cdot\;)$ and $\beta=\tr(\sigma\;\cdot\;)$ be faithful states on $\A$ and $\B$, respectively, and let $\rho$ and $\sigma$ be their corresponding density matrices. Choose an orthogonal eigenvalue decomposition of $\rho$ and $\sigma$. Let $U_{\rho}:\mathbb{T}^{m}\to\mathcal{U}(m)$ and $U_{\sigma}:\mathbb{T}^{n}\to\mathcal{U}(n)$ be representations of the form in Definition~[ref:defn:stateunitaries].
Let $(\B,\beta)\xrightarrow{F}(\A,\alpha)$ be a state-preserving CPU map.

-
The map $F$ is with respect to the representations $U_{\rho}$ and $U_{\sigma}$, or iff

$$

\Ad_{U^{\vartheta}_{\rho}}\circ F=F\circ \Ad_{U^{\varphi}_{\sigma}}

$$

for all $\vartheta\in[0,2\pi]^{m}$ and $\varphi\in[0,2\pi]^{n}$.

-
The associated to the above data is the state-preserving CPU map $(\A,\alpha)\xrightarrow{\mathcal{R}^{\varphi,\vartheta}_{\rho,F}}(\B,\beta)$ given by

$$

\mathcal{R}^{\varphi,\vartheta}_{\rho,F}=\Ad_{U^{\varphi}_{\sigma}}\circ\Ad_{\sigma^{-1/2}}\circ F^*\circ \Ad_{\rho^{1/2}}\circ\Ad_{U^{\vartheta\dag}_{\rho}}.

$$

## Lemma

Given the data in Definition~[ref:defn:covarianceandrotatedPetz], if $F$ is covariant with respect to the representations $U_{\rho}$ and $U_{\sigma}$, then $F$ satisfies the Accardi--Cecchini condition.

We prove this result because we will later use some of the ingredients that appear in the proof.

## Proof

Let $\rho=\sum_{k=1}^{m}p_{k}P_{k}$ and $\sigma=\sum_{l=1}^{n}q_{l}Q_{l}$ be an orthogonal decomposition of $\rho$ and $\sigma$, respectively, and define the maps

$$

\begin{split}
\RR&\xrightarrow{\mathcal{I}_{\rho}}\mathbb{T}^{m}\\

t&\mapsto t\big(\ln(p_{1}),\dots,\ln(p_{m})\big)
\end{split}

$$

and

$$

\begin{split}
\RR&\xrightarrow{\mathcal{I}_{\sigma}}\mathbb{T}^{n}\\

t&\mapsto t\big(\ln(q_{1}),\dots,\ln(q_{n})\big)
\end{split}

$$

where it is understood that each entry is defined modulo $2\pi$. Using the fact that

$$

\rho^{it}
=e^{it\log(\rho)}
=\sum_{k=1}^{m}e^{it\log(p_{k})}P_{k}
\quad\text{ and }\quad
\sigma^{it}
=e^{it\log(\sigma)}
=\sum_{l=1}^{n}e^{it\log(q_{l})}Q_{l}

$$

for all $t\in\RR$,

$$

\Ad_{\rho^{it}}\circ F
=\Ad_{U^{\mathcal{I}_{\rho}(t)}_{\rho}}\circ F
=F\circ\Ad_{U^{\mathcal{I}_{\sigma}(t)}_{\sigma}}\\
=F\circ\Ad_{\sigma^{it}},

$$

where we have used $(U_{\rho},U_{\sigma})$-covariance in the second equality.

## Disintegrations, conditional expectations, and Takesaki's theorem

...

Consider now $\Phi$ a CPU map from $\mathcal{M}$ to itself, such that $\varphi \circ \Phi=\varphi$, where $\varphi$ is a state on $\mathcal{M}$. Let $\Phi$ be Bayes invertible, with Bayes inverse $\Phi^\flat$. In this case $\varphi \circ \Phi^\flat = \varphi$. We define $$\mathfrak{E}(A):=\lim_{N \rightarrow \infty} \frac{1}{N}\sum_{j=1}^{N}\Phi^j(A).$$ Note that $\mathfrak{E}$ is Bayes invertible as well, with Bayes inverse $\mathfrak{E}^\flat(A)=\lim_{N \rightarrow \infty} \frac{1}{N}\sum_{j=1}^{N}\Phi^{\flat^j}(A)$ $\varphi-$a.e.. We generalize 3.1 in [cite:CaVe20].

## Lemma

A density matrix $\tau \in \mathcal{M}$ satisfies $\Phi(\tau)=\tau$ $\varphi-$a.e. if and only if $\mathfrak{E}(\tau)=\tau$ $\varphi-$a.e..

## Proof

Note that $\varphi(\tau A)=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{j=1}^{N}\varphi(\Phi^j(\tau)A)=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{j=1}^{N}\varphi(\tau\Phi^{\flat^j}(A))$. In the limit, we have $\varphi(\tau A)=\varphi(\tau \mathfrak{E}^\flat(A))=\varphi(\mathfrak{E}(\tau) A)$, so that $\tau=\mathfrak{E}^\flat(\tau)$ $\varphi-$a.e.. On the other hand, we note that $\mathfrak{E}^\flat \circ \Phi^\flat=\Phi^\flat \circ \mathfrak{E}^\flat= \mathfrak{E}^\flat$ $\varphi$-a.e. so that

$$\varphi(\tau A)=\varphi(\mathfrak{E}(\tau)A)=\varphi(\tau \mathfrak{E}^\flat(A))=\varphi(\tau \mathfrak{E}^\flat(\Phi^\flat(A)))=\varphi(\tau \Phi^\flat(A))=\varphi(\Phi(\tau)A).$$

## Remark

If $\varphi$ is a faithful state, then the Bayes inverse is unique and $\varphi$-a.e. equivalences become actual identities.

## Remark

In the case where $\varphi=\tr$, we have Lemma 3.1. in [cite:CaVe20].

## Definition [label:defn:classicalconditionalexpectation]

Let $(X,\Sigma,p)$ be a probability space with $\sigma$-algebra $\Sigma$ and let $\Lambda\subseteq\Sigma$ be a sub $\sigma$-algebra. Let $\varphi:(X,\Sigma)\to\RR$ be a measurable function

Such measurable functions are sometimes called , though we avoid this terminology.

(the $\sigma$-algebra on $\RR$ is always taken to be the Borel $\sigma$-algebra unless otherwise stated) that is $p$-integrable ( $\varphi$ has finite $p$-expectation). Let $(X,\Sigma)\xrightarrow{f}(X,\Lambda)$ denote the measurable map whose underlying function on sets is the identity function on $X$, i.e., $f(x)=x$ for all $x\in X$, and let $p_{\restriction\Lambda}$ denote the restriction of the probability measure $p$ to $\Lambda$ (equivalently, $p_{\restriction\Lambda}$ is the pushforward of $p$ along $f$)---these data are summarized by the diagram

$$

\xy0;/r.25pc/:
(0,7.5)*+{\{\bullet\}}="o";
(-10,-7.5)*+{(X,\Sigma)}="X";
(10,-7.5)*+{(X,\Lambda)}="Y";
{\ar@{~>}"o";"X"_{p}};
{\ar@{~>}"o";"Y"^{p_{\restriction\Lambda}}};
{\ar"X";"Y"_{f}};
{\ar@{=}(-2,-3);(2,-1)},
\endxy

$$

in the category $\Mker$ of measurable spaces and Markov kernels.
A is a $p_{\restriction\Lambda}$-integrable function $\EE[\varphi|\Lambda]:(X,\Lambda)\to\RR$ such that

$$

\int_{B}\EE[\varphi|\Lambda]\;dp_{\restriction\Lambda}=\int_{B}\varphi\;dp

$$

for all $B\in\Lambda$.

Note that if we had a measurable function $\psi:(X,\Lambda)\to\RR$, we could easily pull back $\psi$ along $f$ to obtain a measurable function $\psi\circ f:(X,\Sigma)\to\RR$. Thus, a conditional expectation provides a method of pushing forward a measurable function.

## Example [label:ex:conditionalexpectationdiscrete]

We begin with an overly simple example. Let $X:=\NN$ and let $\Sigma$ be the discrete $\sigma$-algebra. Let $\Lambda$ be the $\sigma$-algebra generated by subsets of $X$ of the form $\{x_{2n-1},x_{2n}\}_{n\in\NN}$. Let $p$ be a probability measure on $(X,\Sigma)$ and let $p_{\restriction\Lambda}$ be its pushforward under $f$. One can visualize this as

where the generating measurable subsets have been drawn as bubbles (the sizes do not reflect the associated probabilities, which could be arbitrary). Let $p_{n}$ denote the probability $p(\{x_{n}\})$. Then $p_{\restriction\Lambda}(\{x_{2n-1},x_{2n}\})=p_{2n-1}+p_{2n}.$ For simplicity, suppose that $p$ is nowhere vanishing. Now, given a $\Sigma$-measurable function $\varphi$, its conditional expectation is given by

$$

\EE[\varphi|\Lambda](x_{2n-1})\equiv\EE[\varphi|\Lambda](x_{2n})=\frac{\varphi(x_{2n-1})p_{2n-1}+\varphi(x_{2n})p_{2n}}{p_{2n-1}+p_{2n}}

$$

for all $n\in\NN$. In other words, $\EE[\varphi|\Lambda]$ is a function that is constant on each set of the form $\{x_{2n-1},x_{2n}\}\in\Lambda$ and the value on the elements of that given set is the average of its values on those elements weighted by their probabilities $p_{2n-1}$ and $p_{2n}$.

Conditional expectations exist and are almost everywhere unique. To make this precise, and to sketch the idea, we recall the Radon--Nikodym theorem suitable for our purposes. Recall that if $p$ and $q$ are measures on $(X,\Sigma)$, then $q$ is $p$, written $q\ll p$, iff $p(E)=0$ for any $E\in\Sigma$ implies $q(E)=0$.

## Theorem [label:thm:RN]

Let $(X,\Sigma)$ be a measurable space and let $p$ be a finite measure on $(X,\Sigma)$ ( $p(X)<\infty$).

-
If $\varphi:(X,\Sigma)\to\RR_{\ge0}$ is a measurable function that is $p$-integrable, then the measure $q:=\varphi\cdot p$ defined by

$$
\Sigma\ni E\mapsto
q(E):=\int_E\varphi\, dp
$$

satisfies $q\ll p.$

-
If $q$ is another finite measure on $(X,\Sigma)$ such that $q\ll p$, then there exists a $p$-integrable function $\varphi:(X,\Sigma)\to\RR_{\ge0}$ such that $\varphi\cdot p=q$. Furthermore, if $\psi$ is another $p$-integrable function such that $\psi\cdot p=q$, then $\psi$ is $p$-a.e.\ equal to $\varphi$.

## Proof

For a proof of a more general case, see [cite:Fo99].

The function $\varphi$ in the Radon--Nikodym theorem is called a and will be denoted by $\frac{dq}{dp}$. If one is working with a.e.\ equivalence classes of functions, which will often be the case, it will be referred to as the Radon--Nikodym derivative.

The Radon--Nikodym derivative is used to prove the existence of conditional expecations. In addition, we list several properties of conditional expectations to further illuminate that conditionals expectations in the measure theory sense are also conditional expectations in the operator algebraic sense, which will be defined shortly afterwards.

## Corollary [label:cor:propertiesofconditionalexpectations]

Let $X,\Sigma,p,\Lambda,f,p_{\restriction\Lambda},$ and $\varphi$ be as in Definition~[ref:defn:classicalconditionalexpectation].

-
A conditional expectation of $\varphi$ with respect to $\Lambda$ exists.

-
A conditional expectation is $p_{\restriction\Lambda}$-a.e.\ unique.

-
The assignment

$$

\begin{split}
L^{\infty}(X,\Sigma,p)&\xrightarrow{\EE[\;\cdot\;|\Lambda]}L^{\infty}(X,\Lambda,p_{\restriction\Lambda})\\
\varphi&\xmapsto{\qquad\;}\EE[\varphi|\Lambda]
\end{split}

$$

is a (well-defined) normal positive (linear) unital map satisfying

$$

\EE[\psi\varphi|\Lambda]=\psi\EE[\varphi|\Lambda]

$$

for all $\psi\in L^{\infty}(X,\Lambda,p_{\restriction\Lambda})$ and $\varphi\in L^{\infty}(X,\Sigma,p)$. Here, concatenation denotes multiplication.

-

$\EE[\psi|\Lambda]=\psi$ for all $\psi\in L^{\infty}(X,\Lambda,p_{\restriction\Lambda})$, or equivalently, the diagram

$$

\xy0;/r.25pc/:
(-20,-7.5)*+{L^{\infty}(X,\Lambda,p_{\restriction\Lambda})}="pr";
(20,-7.5)*+{L^{\infty}(X,\Lambda,p_{\restriction\Lambda})}="pr2";
(0,7.5)*+{L^{\infty}(X,\Sigma,p)}="p";
{\ar"pr";"p"^{L^{\infty}(f)}};
{\ar@{~>}"p";"pr2"^{\EE[\;\cdot\;|\Lambda]}};
{\ar"pr";"pr2"^{id}};
\endxy

$$

commutes, where $L^{\infty}(f)$ takes $\varphi\in L^{\infty}(X,\Lambda,p_{\restriction\Lambda})$ to the equivalence class of $\varphi\circ f$ upon choosing a representative. In particular, $L^{\infty}(f):L^{\infty}(X,\Lambda,p_{\restriction\Lambda})\to L^{\infty}(X,\Sigma,p)$ is injective so that the conditional expectation map $\EE[\;\cdot\;|\Lambda]$ is an idempotent mapping when viewed as a map from $L^{\infty}(X,\Sigma,p)$ to itself due to the inclusion of $L^{\infty}(X,\Lambda,p_{\restriction\Lambda})$ inside $L^{\infty}(X,\Sigma,p)$, i.e.,

$$

\EE\big[\EE[\varphi|\Lambda]|\Lambda]\big]=\EE[\varphi|\Lambda] \qquad \forall\; \varphi\in L^{\infty}(X,\Sigma,p).

$$
