This result motivated Umegaki to define conditional expectations for von~Neumann algebras. To appreciate this generalization, we will first review some results regarding abelian von~Neumann algebras. We now recall the operator algebraic definition of a conditional expectation so that we can relate disintegrations, (probabilistic) conditional expectations, and (operator algebraic) conditional expectations.

## Definition [label:defn:conditionalexpectation]

Let $\mathcal{M}$ and $\mathcal{N}$ be von~Neumann algebras (or more generally $C^*$-algebras), with $\mathcal{N}\subseteq \mathcal{M}$. A (sometimes called an to distinguish it from the probabilistic notion introduced earlier) is a linear map $E: \mathcal{M} \stoch \mathcal{M}$ such that

- $E$ is a onto $\mathcal{N}$, i.e., $E(n)=n$ for all $n \in \mathcal{N}$,

- $E$ is , i.e. $E(n x)= n E(x) $ for all $n \in \mathcal{N}, \ x \in \mathcal{M}$, and

- $E$ is positive.

If $\omega:\M\stoch\CC$ is a normal weight, let $\omega_{\restriction\N}$ denote its restriction to $\N$. A conditional expectation is one such that $\omega_{\restriction\N}\circ E=\omega$.

## Remark

Since a conditional expectation $E$ is positive, it is $*$-preserving. As such, left $\N$-modularity of $E$ implies right $\N$-modularity. Indeed, if $E$ is left $\N$-modular, then $E(xn)=E(n^*x^*)^{*}=(n^*E(x^*))^*=E(x)n$ for all $x\in\M$ and $n\in\N$. Hence, $E$ is in the sense that $E(n_1 x n_2)= n_1 E(x) n_2$ for all $n_1,n_2 \in \mathcal{N}, \ x \in \mathcal{M}$,

## Theorem: Tomiyama~ 57

(Tomiyama 1957) Every projection of norm $1$ from $\mathcal{M}$ to $\mathcal{N}$ is a conditional expectation and vice-versa.

## Proof

See~[cite:St81].

## Remark

A conditional expectation is automatically completely positive. In particular, it is a unital , meaning that $E(x^* x) \geq E(x)^*E(x)$ for all $x \in \mathcal{M}$.

An immediate consequence of Corollary~[ref:cor:propertiesofconditionalexpectations] is the following result, which says that a measure theoretic conditional expectation is an example of an operator algebraic conditional expectation.

## Corollary [label:cor:expectationsalgandprob]

Let $X,\Sigma,p,\Lambda,f,$ and $p_{\restriction\Lambda}$ be as in Definition~[ref:defn:classicalconditionalexpectation].
Then $\mathbb{E}[\;\cdot\;|\Lambda]$ is a state-preserving (operator algebraic) conditional expectation with respect to the subalgebra inclusion $L^{\infty}(X,\Lambda,p_{\restriction\Lambda})\subseteq L^{\infty}(X,\Sigma,p)$.
Conversely, if $E$ is a state-preserving operator algebraic conditional expectation with respect to this subalgebra inclusion, then $E(\varphi)$ is a conditional expectation of $\varphi$ with respect to $\Lambda$ for all $\varphi\in L^{\infty}(X,\Sigma,p)$.

## Proof

The first claim was proved in Corollary~[ref:cor:propertiesofconditionalexpectations]. As for the second claim, one must prove $\int_{B}E(\varphi)\,dp_{\restriction\Lambda}=\int_{B}\varphi\,dp$ for arbitrary $B\in\Lambda$ by the a.e.\ uniqueness of Radon--Nikodym derivatives. Furthermore, it suffices to let $\varphi=\chi_{A}$ with $A\in\Sigma$ by the density of simple functions in $L^{\infty}(X,\Sigma,p)$. In this case,

$$

\int_{B}E(\chi_{A})\,dp_{\restriction\Lambda}
=\int_{X}\chi_{B}E(\chi_{A})\,dp_{\restriction\Lambda}
=\int_{X}E(\chi_{B}\chi_{A})\,dp_{\restriction\Lambda}\\

=\int_{X}\chi_{B}\chi_{A}\,dp
=\int_{B}\chi_{A}\,dp

$$

by the defining properties of a state-preserving algebraic conditional expectation.

In the following, let $(X,\mu)$ be a finite measure space. However, the proofs can be altered to account for a $\sigma$-finite measure space.

## Lemma

There exists an isometric *-homomorphism
$$
M:\mathcal{L}^\infty(X,\mu)\rightarrow B(\mathcal{L}^2(X,\mu)),\quad M(g)=M_g
$$
where $M_g$ is a multiplication operator on $\mathcal{L}^2$. Under this mapping we can view $L^\infty(X,\mu)$ as a *-subalgebra of $B(\mathcal{L}^2(X,\mu))$.

## Theorem

$\mathcal{L}^\infty(X,\mu)$ is a von-Neumann algebra.

## Proof [label:eq:chareq]

Let $M=M(\mathcal{L}^\infty(X,\mu))\subset\mathcal{L}^2(X,\mu)$ and let $T\in M''$. By the bi-commutant theorem it is enough to show that $M''\subset M$. We note that all characteristics functions are in $\mathcal{L}^\infty(X,\mu)$. Define, $f=T(1)$, where $1\in \mathcal{L}^2(X,\mu)$. Since $M$ is abelian, $M\subset M'$ and therefore

$$
T(\chi_E)=TM_{\chi_E}(1)=M_{\chi_E}T(1)=M_{\chi_E}f=f\chi_E
$$

where $\chi_E$ is a characteristic function and the middle equality is due to the fact $T\in M''$ and $M_{\chi_E}\in M\subset M'$. We now assert that $T(g)=f\cdot g$ i.e. that $T$ is given by multiplication by $f$ and that $f\in \mathcal{L}^\infty(X,\mu)$. Since $T$ was arbitrary, this shows that $T\in M''$ implies that $T\in M$. The first part of the assertion is trivial since [ref:eq:chareq] shows by linearity $T$ is multiplication by $f$ on simple functions. Simple functions are dense in $\mathcal{L}^2(X,\mu)$ and $T$ is a bounded operator. Thus we simply prove that $f\in \mathcal{L}^\infty(X,\mu)$. For any fixed $\varepsilon>0$, the measure of the set

$$
A=\{x : |f(x)|\geq \esssup |f|-\varepsilon\}
$$
is greater than zero, i.e. $\mu(A)>0$.

$$

\|T\chi_A\|_2=\sqrt{\int_A|f|^2\, d\mu}\geq \mu(A)\cdot(\esssup|f|-\varepsilon)

$$

Thus,

$$

\|T\|_{\text{op}}
=\sup_{\psi\in\mathcal{L}^2}\frac{\|T\psi\|_2}{\|\psi\|_2}
\geq \frac{\|T\chi_{A}\|_2}{\|\chi_A\|_2}
\geq \esssup|f|-\varepsilon.

$$

The above is true for all $\varepsilon>0$, thus $\|f\|_\infty\leq \|T\|_{\text{op}}$.

We can actually show that $\|f\|_{\infty}=\|T\|_{\text{op}}$, but this is unnecessary for the above.

## Classical disintegrations and conditional expectations

How are conditional expectations and disintegrations of $(X,\Sigma,p)\xrightarrow{f}(X,\Lambda,p_{\restriction\Lambda})$ related? To better explain the relationships, we will review Markov kernels and their $L^{\infty}$ von~Neumann algebra analogues, positive unital maps.

## Definition [label:defn:transitionkernel]

Let $(X,\Sigma)$ and $(Y,\Lambda)$ be measurable spaces.
A
$f$ from $(X,\Sigma)$ to $(Y,\Lambda)$, written $(X,\Sigma)\xstoch{f}(Y,\Lambda)$ (or just $X\xstoch{f}Y$ if the $\sigma$-algebras are clear from context) is a function
$f:X\times\Lambda\to[0,\infty]$ such that

[i.]

-
$f(x,\;\cdot\;):\Lambda\to[0,\infty]$ is a measure for all $x\in X$ and

-
$f(\;\cdot\;,E):X\to[0,\infty]$ is measurable for all $E\in\Lambda.$

The notation $f_{x}(E):=f(x,E)$ will be implemented.
A transition kernel $f$ is (resp.\ a ) iff $f_{x}(E)\in\{0,1\}$ (resp.\ $f_{x}(E)\in[0,1]$) for all $x\in X$ and $E\in\Lambda$.
If $(X,\Sigma)$ is equipped with a measure $\mu$, then $f$ is (resp.\ a ) iff for each $E\in\Lambda$, there exists an $N_{E}\in\Sigma$ such that $\mu(N_{E})=0$, termed a , and $f_{x}(E)\in\{0,1\}$ (resp.\ $f_{x}(E)\in[0,1]$) for all $x\in X\setminus N_{E}$.

## Definition [label:defn:compositionoftransitionkernels]

Let $(X,\Sigma),$ $(Y,\Lambda),$ and $(Z,\Omega)$ be measurable spaces.
Let $X\xstoch{f}Y$ and $Y\xstoch{g}Z$ be two transition kernels.
The of $f$ followed by $g,$
written as $g\circ f:X\stoch Z,$ is the transition kernel defined by

$$

X\times\Omega\ni(x,E)\mapsto(g\circ f)_{x}(E)
:=\int_{Y}g_{y}(E)\,df_{x}(y).

$$

## Definition [label:defn:aeequivalencetransitionkernels]

Let $(X,\Sigma,\mu)$ be a measure space and let $(Y,\Lambda)$ be a measurable space.
Two transition kernels $f,g:(X,\Sigma)\to (Y,\Lambda)$ are said to be
, written as
$f\aeequals{\mu}g,$
iff for each $E\in\Lambda,$ there exists a $\mu$-nullset $N_{E}$ such that $f_{x}(E)=g_{x}(E)$ for all $x\in X\setminus N_{E}.$

## Remark

In terms of the notation from Definition~[ref:defn:aeequivalencetransitionkernels], $f\aeequals{\mu}g$ holds if and only if

$$

\endxy
,\quad\text{i.e.}\quad

,

$$

where the string diagrams on the right are identified with the morphisms on the left, which are morphisms in the category of Markov kernels. The map $\Delta_{X}$ is the diagonal map.

## Lemma [label:lem:aeclassesofmkcompose]

Let $(X,\Sigma,\mu), (Y,\Lambda,\nu), (Z,\Omega,\lambda)$ be finite measure spaces and let $f,f':(X,\Sigma,\mu)\to(Y,\Lambda,\nu)$ and $g,g':(Y,\Lambda,\nu)\to(Z,\Omega,\lambda)$ be two pairs of Markov kernels such that $f\aeequals{\mu}f'$ and $g\aeequals{\nu}g'$. Then $g\circ f\aeequals{\mu} g'\circ f'$.

## Proof

This follows more abstractly from the fact that the category of Markov kernels is causal~[cite:Fr20], but we can give a direct proof as well. First note that $g\circ f\aeequals{\mu} g\circ f'$ immediately follows from the equivalent diagrammatic definition of a.e.\ equivalence. Hence, it suffices to prove $g\circ f'\aeequals{\mu}g'\circ f'$. To see this, let $C\in\Omega$. Since $g\aeequals{\nu}g'$, there exists an $N_{C}\in\Lambda$ such that $\nu(N_{C})=0$ and $g_{y}(C)=g'_{y}(C)$ for all $y\in Y\setminus N_{C}$. Since $f'\circ\mu=\nu$, we have $0=\nu(N_{C})=\int_{X}f'_{x}(N_{C})\,d\mu(x)$. Since the integrand and measure here are non-negative, there exists an $M_{C}\in\Sigma$ such that $\mu(M_{C})=0$ and $f'_{x}(N_{C})=0$ for all $x\in X\setminus M_{C}$. Thus,

$$

\begin{split}
(g\circ f')_{x}(C)&=\int_{Y\setminus N_{C}}g_{y}(C)\,df'_{x}(y)+\int_{N_{C}}g_{y}(C)\,df_{x}'(y)\\
&=\int_{Y\setminus N_{C}}g'_{y}(C)\,df'_{x}(y)+\int_{N_{C}}g_{y}(C)\,df_{x}'(y)\\
&=\int_{Y}g'_{y}(C)\,df'_{x}(y)
\end{split}

$$

for all $x\in X\setminus M_{C}$.
Thus, $g\circ f\aeequals{\mu} g\circ f'\aeequals{\mu}g'\circ f'.$

## Corollary

There is a category of probability spaces and a.e.\ equivalence classes of Markov kernels. More precisely, the objects are probability spaces $(X,\Sigma,p)$ and morphisms are a.e.\ equivalence classes of measure-preserving Markov kernels.

## Remark

The definition of a.e.\ equivalence in Definition~[ref:defn:aeequivalencetransitionkernels] is a bit subtle. Another reasonable option would be to say $f$ and $g$ are $\mu$-a.e.\ equivalent iff there exists an $N\in\Sigma$ such that $f_{x}=g_{x}$ (equality of measures) for all $x\in X\setminus N$ and $\mu(N)=0$. This second option implies Definition~[ref:defn:aeequivalencetransitionkernels], but the converse is not true in general.

## Lemma [label:lem:Linftyfunctor]

Let $(X,\Sigma,\mu)$ and $(Y,\Lambda,\nu)$ be finite measure spaces and let $(X,\Sigma)\xrightarrow{f}(Y,\Lambda)$ be a measure-preserving Markov kernel, i.e., $\nu=f\circ \mu$.

-
The assignment

$$

\begin{split}
L^{\infty}(Y,\Lambda,\nu)&\xrightarrow{L^{\infty}(f)} L^{\infty}(X,\Sigma,\mu)\\
\varphi&\xmapsto{\qquad\;}\left[X\ni x\mapsto\int_{Y}\varphi\,df_{x}\right]
\end{split}

$$

is a normal positive (linear) unital map.

-
If $f$ is a measurable function, then $L^{\infty}(f)$ is a (normal) unital $*$-homomorphism, which is given by the pullback map sending $\varphi\in L^{\infty}(Y,\Lambda,\nu)$ to $\varphi\circ f$ (upon choosing a representative for $\varphi$ and then taking the $\mu$-a.e.\ equivalence class). More generally,
$L^{\infty}(f)$ is a (normal) unital $*$-homomorphism if and only if $f$ is $\mu$-a.e.\ deterministic.

-
$L^{\infty}$ defines a functor

$$

\mathbf{FMMK}^{\op}\xrightarrow{L^{\infty}}\mathbf{cvNAlgNPU}

$$

from (the opposite of the category of) finite measure spaces and measure-preserving Markov kernels to commutative von~Neumann algebras and normal positive unital maps.

-

If $\omega:L^{\infty}(X,\Sigma,\mu)\to\mathbb{C}$ and $\xi:L^{\infty}(Y,\Lambda,\nu)\to\mathbb{C}$ are the weights associated to $\mu$ and $\nu$, respectively, then $\omega\circ L^{\infty}(f)=\xi$.

-

If $(X,\Sigma)\xrightarrow{g}(Y,\Lambda)$ is another Markov kernel satisfying $f\aeequals{\mu}g$, then $L^{\infty}(f)=L^{\infty}(g)$.

-
The functor $L^{\infty}$ is fully faithful if $(Y,\Lambda,\nu)$ is a standard Borel space or a standard Lebesgue space. ( ) --- I think faithfulness is false if we don't mod out by a.e.\ equivalence on the domain category. However, is the composite of a.e.\ equivalence classes of markov kernels well-defined? This was a question I could not answer for our disintegration paper---Answer: Yes, Lemma~[ref:lem:aeclassesofmkcompose] above proves this! So doesn't this mean the $L^{\infty}$ functor descends to a quotiented category of a.e.\ equivalence classes of Markov kernels?

## Proof

-
We break the proof of this into several parts by first discussing the well-definedness of this assignment, then proving positivity and normality.

[(a)]

-
Let $\varphi$ be an essentially bounded extended complex-valued function on $(Y,\Lambda,\nu)$. Thus, there exists a $\nu$-null set $B\in\Lambda$ and a constant $c\in[0,\infty)$ such that $|\varphi(y)|\le c$ for all $y\in Y\setminus B$. Since $\varphi_{\restriction Y\setminus B}$ is $\CC$-valued, there exist a decomposition $\varphi_{\restriction Y\setminus B}=\varphi_{+}^{\mathfrak{Re}}-\varphi_{-}^{\mathfrak{Re}}+i\varphi_{+}^{\mathfrak{Im}}-i\varphi_{-}^{\mathfrak{Im}}$ into $[0,\infty)$-valued measurable functions. By the assumption that $\nu=f\circ\mu$, the measure of $B$ satisfies $0=\nu(B)=\int_{X}f_{x}(B)\,d\mu(x)$. Since the integrand is non-negative and $\mu$ is a non-negative measure, this implies there exists a $\mu$-null set $M\in\Sigma$ such that $f_{x}(B)=0$ for all $x\in X\setminus M$. Define a function $f^{*}\varphi$ on $X$ by

$$

X\ni x\mapsto\begin{cases}\int_{Y\setminus B}\varphi\,df_{x}&\mbox{ for $x\in X\setminus M$}\\0&\mbox{ for $x\in M$}\end{cases}
.

$$

Note that $f^*\varphi$ is a measurable $\CC$-valued function. This follows from the fact that if $\varphi_{\restriction Y\setminus B}$ were non-negative, then there exists an increasing sequence of simple functions $\NN\ni n\mapsto s_{n}$ on $(Y,\Lambda)$ that converges pointwise to $\varphi_{\restriction Y\setminus B}$. By the definition of the integral, $\int_{Y}\varphi_{\restriction Y\setminus B}\,df_{x}=\lim_{n\to\infty}\int_{Y}s_{n}\,df_{x}=:\lim_{n\to\infty}t_{n}(x)$, where $\NN\ni n\mapsto t_{n}$ is an increasing sequence of non-negative measurable functions on $(X,\Sigma)$. Thus, the limit gives a measurable function. For an arbitrary $\varphi$, break it up into a complex combination of four non-negative terms and apply the previous argument to each part. Thus, $f^{*}\varphi$ is measurable. From this, it follows that $f^{*}\varphi$ is essentially bounded because $\left|\int_{Y\setminus B}\varphi\,df_{x}\right|\le\int_{Y\setminus B}|\varphi|\,df_{x}=cf_{x}(Y\setminus B)\le c$ for all $x\in X\setminus M$ (since $f_{x}$ is a probability measure). Now suppose that $\psi$ is another essentially bounded extended complex-valued function on $(Y,\Lambda,\nu)$ that is $\nu$-a.e.\ equivalent to $\varphi$. Let $A$ be a $\nu$-null set and let $d\in[0,\infty)$ be a constant such that $|\psi(y)|\le d$ for all $y\in Y\setminus A$. Let $N$ be a $\mu$-null set over which $f^{*}\psi$ is defined by a similar integral formula above. Finally, let $E$ be a $\nu$-null set such that $\varphi(y)=\psi(y)$ for all $y\in Y\setminus E$. Since $\nu(A\cup B\cup E)=0$, we get

$$

\int_{Y\setminus B}\varphi\,df_{x}
=\int_{Y\setminus(A\cup B\cup E)}\varphi\,df_{x}
=\int_{Y\setminus(A\cup B\cup E)}\psi\,df_{x}
=\int_{Y\setminus A}\psi\,df_{x}

$$

for all $x\in X\setminus(M\cup N)$ proving that $f^{*}\varphi$ is $\mu$-a.e.\ equivalent to $f^{*}\psi$. Putting these results proves that $L^{\infty}(f):L^{\infty}(Y,\Omega,\nu)\to L^{\infty}(X,\Sigma,\mu)$ is a well-defined function.

-
If $\varphi$ is real non-negative then its integral with respect to $f_{x}$ is always non-negative. Unitality follows from $f_{x}$ being a probability measure.

The following argument was explained to me by Robert Furber on zulip: . Note that a similar argument to what follows can be adapted to $\sigma$-finite measure spaces.

consider a directed subset of $\nu$-a.e.\ equivalence classes of characteristic functions $\chi_{B_{\beta}}$ with $B_{\beta}\in\Lambda$ such that $\chi_{B}=\lim_{\beta\to\infty}\chi_{B_{\beta}}$ for some $B\in\Lambda$ (we are using the fact that the supremum of a direct set of projections in a von~Neumann algebra is a projection~[cite:AAWe19] and that every projection in $L^{\infty}(Y,\Omega,\nu)$ is of this form~[cite:AAWe19]). It suffices to consider such a net where the symmetric difference

$$

B_{\beta}\triangle B_{\beta'}:=(B_{\beta}\cup B_{\beta'})\setminus(B_{\beta}\cap B_{\beta'})

$$

has strictly positive $\nu$ measure for all $\beta<\beta'$ (if this were not the case, then $\chi_{B_{\beta}}$ would be $\nu$-a.e.\ equivalent to $\chi_{B_{\beta'}}$ and hence equal as projection elements in $L^{\infty}(Y,\Omega,\nu)$). The net $C_{\beta}:=B_{\beta}\setminus\left(\bigcup_{\gamma<\beta}B_{\gamma}\right)$ thus defines a net of disjoint strictly positive $\nu$-measure sets whose sum is $\nu(B)\le\nu(Y)<\infty$. This is only possible if the net is at most countable since an uncountable sum of strictly positive numbers is infinite. Therefore, it suffices to consider a bounded increasing sequence of projections $\NN\ni n\mapsto\chi_{B_{n}}\in L^{\infty}(Y,\Omega,\nu)$. The functions $X\ni x\mapsto\int_{Y}\chi_{B_{n}}\,df_{x}=f_{x}(B_{n})$ form an increasing sequence of measurable functions bounded from above by $1$. By Lebesgue's monotone convergence theorem (cf.\ [cite:Ru87]), this sequence converges to the (a.e.\ equivalence class represented by the) function $X\ni x\mapsto f_{x}(B)=\int_{Y}\chi_{B}\,df_{x}$. This proves that $L^{\infty}(f)$ is normal.

More generally, suppose that $f$ is $\mu$-a.e.\ deterministic. In what follows, we will show that for characteristic functions $\chi_{E},\chi_{F}\in L^{\infty}(Y,\Lambda,\nu)$, $L^{\infty}(f)(\chi_{E}\chi_{F})=\big(L^{\infty}(f)(\chi_{E})\big)\big(L^{\infty}(f)(\chi_{F})\big)$. By assumption, there exists a $\mu$-nullset
$N$ such that
$f_{x}(E),f_{x}(F),f_{x}(E\cap F),f_{x}(E\triangle F)\in\{0,1\}$ for all $x\in X\setminus N.$
Since $E\cap F\subseteq E,F$, if either $f_{x}(E)$ or $f_{x}(F)$ is $0$, then $f_{x}(E\cap F)=0$. Hence, consider the case $f_{x}(E)=1=f_{x}(F)$. If $f_{x}(E\cap F)=0$, then $f_{x}(E\triangle F)=f_{x}(E)+f_{x}(F)=2$, a contradiction. Hence, $f_{x}(E\cap F)=1$. In both of these cases, $f_{x}(E\cap F)=f_{x}(E)f_{x}(F)$, which proves the claim. Since simple functions are dense in $L^{\infty}(Y,\Lambda,\nu)$, $L^{\infty}(f)$ is a $*$-homomorphism.

Conversely, suppose that $L^{\infty}(f)$ is a $*$-homomorphism, i.e.,

$$
[L^\infty(f)](\varphi\cdot \psi)=[L^\infty(f)](\varphi)\cdot [L^\infty(f)](\psi)

for all $\varphi,\psi\in L^{\infty}(Y,\Lambda,\nu)$. Fix $E\in\Lambda$. Let both $\varphi$ and $\psi$ be the indicator functions for the set $E$. Then

$$

\begin{split}
\Big[X\ni x\mapsto f_{x}(E)\Big]_{\mu}
&=\left[X\ni x\mapsto\int_Y\chi_E\, df_x\right]_{\mu}

\end{split}

$$

where the brackets signify $\mu$-a.e.\ equivalence classes viewed as elements of $L^{\infty}(X,\Sigma,\mu)$. Hence, $f_{x}(E)=f_{x}(E)^{2}$ for all $x\in X\setminus N$ for some $\mu$-nullset $N$. Thus, $f$ is $\mu$-a.e.\ deterministic.

Hence $L^{\infty}(id_{(X,\Sigma,\mu)})(\varphi)=id_{L^{\infty}(X,\Sigma,\mu)}(\varphi).$ Now suppose that $(X,\Sigma,\mu)\xrightarrow{f}(Y,\Lambda,\nu)\xrightarrow{g}(Z,\Omega,\tau)$ is a pair of composable Markov kernels and let $\varphi\in L^{\infty}(Z,\Omega,\tau)$. &=\big(L^{\infty}(f)\circ L^{\infty}(g)\big)(\varphi)
\end{split}

$$

are $\mu$-a.e.\ equivalent since they're already equal on representatives.

Thus $\omega\circ L^{\infty}(f)=L^{\infty}(p)\circ L^{\infty}(f)=L^{\infty}(f\circ \mu)=L^{\infty}(\nu)=\xi$.

Since $f,g:(X,\Sigma)\rightarrow(Y,\Lambda)$ are two Markov kernels satisfying $f\aeequals{\mu}g$, for any such $E\in\Lambda$, there exists a $\mu$-null set $N_E$ such that

## Example [label:ex:noninjective]

In general, we cannot expect that $L^{\infty}(X,\Lambda,p_{\restriction\Lambda})$ is a von~Neumann subalgebra of $L^{\infty}(X,\Sigma,p)$. To see this,
let $X=\{a,b\}$ be a set consisting of two elements and let $\Sigma$ be the discrete $\sigma$-algebra on $X$, i.e. $\Sigma=\{\varnothing,\{a\},\{b\},X\}$. Let $p$ be the unique probability measure with $p(\{a\})=1$. Let $\Lambda$ be the indiscrete $\sigma$-algebra, i.e. $\Lambda=\{\varnothing,X\}$. Let $\psi:=1_{X}$ (the constant function on $X$) and $\varphi$ be the function on $X$ defined by $\varphi(a)=1$ and $\varphi(b)=0$. Then $\varphi$ and $\psi$ are equal when viewed as elements of $L^{\infty}(X,\Sigma,p)$ since $p(\{x\in X\;:\;\varphi(x)\ne\psi(x)\})=p(\{b\})=0$. However, they are not equal when viewed as elements of $L^{\infty}(X,\Lambda,p_{\restriction\Lambda})$ since the only $p_{\restriction\Lambda}$-null set is $\varnothing$ and thus there does not exist a $p_{\restriction\Lambda}$-null set containing $\{x\in X\;:\;\varphi(x)\ne\psi(x)\}$. In other words, the map $L^{\infty}(f):(X,\Lambda,p_{\restriction\Lambda})\to(X,\Sigma,p)$ is not injective.

## Remark [label:rmk:noninjective]

Nevertheless, one can take $(Z,\Omega,r)$ to be $(\{\bullet\},\Omega,1)$, where $\Omega=\{\varnothing,\{\bullet\}\}$ and $1$ is the unique probability measure on $(Z,\Omega)$. Setting $(Z,\Omega,r)\xrightarrow{h}(X,\Sigma,p)$ to be the unique map sending $\bullet$ to $a$, it follows that the composite $(Z,\Omega,r)\xrightarrow{h}(X,\Sigma,p)\xrightarrow{!_{(X,\Sigma)}}(Z,\Omega,r)$ is the identity and the composite $(X,\Sigma,p)\xrightarrow{!_{(X,\Sigma)}}(Z,\Omega,r)\xrightarrow{h}(X,\Sigma,p)$ is $p$-a.e.\ equal to the identity.

How do we bypass this counter-example in a way that allows us to retain a decent level of generality? For example, if our measure spaces are complete (in the sense that every subset of a measure zero set is measurable), would it work? No, the measure spaces in the above example are complete.

It seems in general that the main issue is that $\Lambda$ and $\Sigma$ do not have the same null-sets. I do not know if it has a name, but perhaps we can consider $\Lambda$ with the null sets from $\Sigma$ thrown in. This does not change any probabilities, we are just adding in more ``impossible" events. This may be too restrictive. ## Remark

The following result seems obvious and it is. However, to say that a property $P$ holds almost everywhere is to say the following:

[1.]

- The set $S$ where the property does not hold is measurable.

- The measure of $S$ is zero.

Hence, in order to avoid the difficulties in the above example [ref:ex:noninjective], we will require $\Lambda$ and $\Sigma$ contain the same null sets.

## Proposition

Let $(X,\Sigma, p)$ and $(X, \Lambda, p\restriction_{\Lambda})$ be two measure spaces with $\Lambda$ as a $\sigma$-sub-algebra of $\Sigma$, with the additional assumption that if $S\in \Sigma$ with $p(S)=0$ then $S\in \Lambda$. If $\varphi, \psi\in L^\infty(X,\Sigma, p)$ where $\varphi\aeequals{p} \psi$, then $\varphi, \psi\in L^\infty(X,\Lambda,p\restriction_\Lambda)$ and $\varphi\aeequals{p\restriction_\Lambda}\psi$.

## Proof

We will only point out that the sets

$$
U_{\varphi}&=\{x\in X: \varphi \text{ is unbounded.}\}\\
U_{\psi}&=\{x\in X: \psi \text{ is unbounded.}\}\\
S&=\{x\in X: \varphi(x)\neq \psi(x)\}
$$

are all measurable in both $(X, \Sigma)$ and $(X,\Lambda)$ and measure zero under both $p$ and $p\restriction_{\Lambda}$.

## Corollary [label:cor:conditionalexpectationsanddisintegrations]

Let $X,\Sigma,p,\Lambda,f,$ and $p_{\restriction\Lambda}$ be as in Definition~[ref:defn:classicalconditionalexpectation]. Let $\omega:=L^{\infty}(p)$ and $\xi:=L^{\infty}(p_{\restriction})$ be the states corresponding to $p$ and $p_{\restriction}$, respectively.

-
The conditional expectation map $\mathbb{E}[\;\cdot\;|\Lambda]$ is a strict disintegration of $(L^{\infty}(f),\omega)$.

-
If there exists a disintegration of $(f,p)$, i.e., a Markov kernel $g:(X,\Lambda)\to(X,\Sigma)$ such that $f\circ g\aeequals{p_{\restriction\Lambda}}id_{(X,\Lambda)}$ and $p=g\circ p_{\restriction\Lambda}$, then $L^{\infty}(g)$ is a state-preserving operator algebraic conditional expectation.

-
In particular (under the same assumptions as in the previous item), $L^{\infty}(g)=\mathbb{E}[\;\cdot\;|\Lambda]$.
In other words, the $L^{\infty}$ functor sends a disintegration of $f:(X,\Sigma,p)\to(X,\Lambda,p_{\restriction\Lambda})$
to the state-preserving conditional expectation of $f$.

you found me!

-
Corollary~[ref:cor:propertiesofconditionalexpectations] item~[ref:item:expectationsareleftinverses] shows $\mathbb{E}[\;\cdot\;|\Lambda]\circ L^{\infty}(f)=id_{L^{\infty}(X,\Lambda,p_{\restriction\Lambda})}$. The state-preserving condition of a disintegration follows from

$$

\big(\xi\circ\mathbb{E}[\;\cdot\;|\Lambda]\big)(\varphi)
=\int_{X}\mathbb{E}[\varphi|\Lambda]\,dp_{\restriction\Lambda}
=\int_{X}\varphi\,dp
=\omega(\varphi)
\qquad\forall\;\varphi\in L^{\infty}(X,\Sigma,p),

$$

where the second equality holds by the defining property of the conditional expecation from Definition~[ref:defn:classicalconditionalexpectation].

-
By Lemma~[ref:lem:Linftyfunctor], $L^{\infty}(g)$ is a normal positive unital map.
Because $L^\infty$ is a contravariant functor,

$$

id_{L^\infty(X,\Lambda,\nu)}=L^{\infty}(id_{(X,\Lambda,\nu)})=L^\infty(f\circ g)=L^\infty(g)\circ L^\infty(f).

$$

The last equality holds by Lemma~[ref:lem:Linftyfunctor] item~[ref:item:aeequivalencesgotosamemap] because $L^{\infty}$ identifies a.e.\ equivalence classes of Markov kernels.
This shows that $L^{\infty}(g)$ is a projection onto the subalgebra $\N:=L^{\infty}(X,\Lambda,p_{\restriction\Lambda})$.
The state-preserving condition follows from Lemma~[ref:lem:Linftyfunctor] item~[ref:item:statepreservingforLinfinity].
The last step is to prove that $E:=L^{\infty}(g)$ is left $\N$-modular, i.e., $E(\psi\varphi)=\psi E(\varphi)$ for all $\psi\in\N$ and $\varphi\in L^{\infty}(X,\Sigma,p)$. Since simple functions are dense in $L^{\infty}$, it suffices to prove the equality for $\psi=\chi_{B}$ with $B\in\Lambda$. By the definition of a consistent disintegration $g_{y}(B)=g_{y}(f^{-1}(B))=\chi_{B}(y)$ for $p_{\restriction\Lambda}$ almost all $y\in X$. Hence,

$$

\begin{split}
(\chi_{B}E(\varphi))(y)
&=\chi_{B}(y)\int_{X}\varphi\,dg_{y}
=\chi_{B}(y)\int_{B}\varphi\,dg_{y}+\chi_{B}(y)\int_{X\setminus B}\varphi\,dg_{y}\\
&=\chi_{B}(y)\int_{B}\varphi\,dg_{y}
=\chi_{B}(y)\int_{X}\chi_{B}\varphi\,dg_{y}
=E(\chi_{B}\varphi)(y),
\end{split}

$$

for $p_{\restriction\Lambda}$ almost all $y\in X$.

This follows from the previous item and the second claim in Corollary~[ref:cor:expectationsalgandprob].

## Example

We continue our simple example from Example~[ref:ex:conditionalexpectationdiscrete] by explicitly constructing a disintegration $(X,\Lambda)\xstoch{g}(X,\Sigma)$. For each $n\in\NN$, let $g_{n}:=g_{x_{n}}$ to avoid double indices. Set

$$

g_{2n-1}(\{x_{m}\})\equiv g_{2n}(\{x_{m}\}):=\begin{cases}\frac{p_{2n-1}}{p_{2n-1}+p_{2n}}&\mbox{if $m=2n-1$}\\\frac{p_{2n}}{p_{2n-1}+p_{2n}}&\mbox{if $m=2n$}\\0&\mbox{otherwise}\end{cases}
.

$$

In other words, $g$ sends $x_{2n-1}$ and $x_{2n}$ to a measure supported on $\{x_{2n-1},x_{2n}\}\in\Sigma$, which is normalized appropriately so that it is a probability measure and so that $p=g\circ p_{\restriction\Lambda}$ holds.

Indeed,

$$

\begin{split}
(g\circ p_{\restriction\Lambda})(\{x_{2n-1}\})
&=\int_{X}g_{x}(\{x_{2n-1}\})\,dp_{\restriction\Lambda}(x)
=\hspace{-6mm}\int\displaylimits_{\{x_{2n-1},x_{2n}\}}\hspace{-6mm}g_{2n}(\{x_{2n-1}\})\,dp_{\restriction\Lambda}(x)\\
&=g_{x}(\{x_{2n-1}\})\hspace{-6mm}\int\displaylimits_{\{x_{2n-1},x_{2n}\}}\hspace{-6mm}dp_{\restriction\Lambda}(x)
=p_{2n-1},
\end{split}

$$

where in the first equality of the second line, we used the fact that $g_{x}(\{x_{2n-1}\})$ is constant in $x$ on the subset $\{x_{2n-1},x_{2n}\}$. Similarly,

$$

(g\circ p_{\restriction\Lambda})(\{x_{2n}\})=p_{2n}.

$$

Thus, $p=g\circ p_{\restriction\Lambda}$. For consistency of $g$, one also needs $id_{(X,\Lambda)}=f\circ g$ (since we are assuming the probability measure is nowhere vanishing). This means for each $y\in X$ and $B\in\Lambda$, the equality $\chi_{y}(B)=\int_{X}f_{x}(B)\,dg_{y}(x)$ must hold. Since $f$ is set theoretically the identity on $X$, this is equivalent to $\chi_{y}(B)=\int_{X}\chi_{B}(x)\,dg_{y}(x)\equiv g_{y}(B)$. But this is immediate from the definition of $g_{y}$ since if $y\in B$, then $g_{y}(B)=1$, and if $y\ne B$, then $g_{y}(B)=0$. This example actually illustrates an interesting situation. The disintegration $g$ is not strongly consistent (in the sense of [cite:FrV4]) because the measure $g_{x}$ is not supported on $f^{-1}(\{x\})$.

## Corollary [label:cor:standardBoreldisint]

Let $X,\Sigma,p,\Lambda,f,p_{\restriction\Lambda},\omega,$ and $\xi$ be as in Lemma~[ref:lem:Linftyfunctor].
Then, the pair $(f,p)$ need not have a disintegration even though the pair $(L^{\infty}(f),\omega)$ always has a disintegration. If, however, the underlying measure spaces are standard Borel or standard Lebesgue, then $(f,p)$ always has a disintegration. More generally, $(f,p)$ has a disintegration if $(X,\Sigma,p)$ is countably compact.

## Proof

For the last claim, see~[cite:FrV4].

## Conditional Expectations in Operator Algebras

## Lemma

Let $\Sigma \supset \Lambda$ be an inclusion of $\sigma-$algebras over the set $X$ and let
$$ \{\cdot \} \xrightarrow{\mu} X \xleftarrow{\nu} \{\cdot \}$$
be finite measures over $\Sigma$ for $\mu$, $\Lambda$ for $\nu$, such that $\nu=\mu_{|\Lambda}$. This can also be stated as the couple $(\mu,\nu)$ preserves the inclusion of measurable spaces $(X,\Lambda)\subset (X,\Sigma)$. \\

Consider all the triangles formed by the triples $(\mu,\nu, id)$ where $\mu, \nu$ as above and $id$ is the associated measurable spaces inclusion.\\

Then the $L^\infty$ functor sends disintegrations to conditional expectations (and vice-versa? Maybe Std. Borel is needed to have full faithfulness). \\

## Proof

Let $g$ be a disintegration of the considered inclusion, then we have that $f\circ g=_{\nu} id$ and that $ g\circ \nu=\mu$, where $f=id$ is the inclusion, so that we have $L^\infty(g): L^\infty(X,\Sigma,\mu) \rightarrow L^\infty(X,\Lambda,\nu)$, $L^\infty(f):L^\infty(X,\Lambda,\nu) \hookrightarrow L^\infty(X,\Sigma,\mu)$ is the inclusion of $L^\infty$ algebras. Because $L^\infty$ is a functor, we have that:\\

- $L^\infty(f\circ g)=L^\infty(g)\circ L^\infty(f)=id_{L^\infty(X,\Lambda,\nu)}$;\\

- we call $\phi_\mu, \phi_\nu$ the functionals associated to the measures (i.e. $L^\infty(\mu),L^\infty(\nu)$, the integrals w.r.t. $\mu$ and $\nu$). Then $\phi_\nu(L^\infty(g)(\cdot))=\phi_\mu(\cdot)$.

From this we have that $L^\infty(g)$ is linear, it is a projection (property 1 above), it is also bimodular, i.e. $\forall \psi_1 , \psi_2 \in L^\infty(X,\Lambda,\nu), \ \varphi \in L^\infty(X,\Sigma,\mu)$ we have that $L^\infty(g)(\psi'_1 \varphi \psi'_2)=\psi_1L^\infty(g)(\varphi)\psi_2 $, where $\psi_i$ is the image of $\psi_i$ under the inclusion. To prove bimodularity, we use the fact that simple functions are dense in $L^\infty(X,\Lambda,\nu)$ and that it suffices to show equivalence of $L^\infty(g)(\psi'_1 \varphi \psi'_2),\psi_1L^\infty(g)(\varphi)\psi_2 $ $\nu-$a.e., also, using the fact that the $L^\infty$ algebras are commutative, the whole bimodularity follows if we prove that $L^\infty(g)(\phi \chi'_A)=L^\infty(g)(\phi)\chi_A, \ \forall A \in \Lambda$. Recalling that $L^\infty(g)(\phi\chi'_A)(x)=\int_{X}\phi\chi'_A dg_x= \int_{A}\phi dg_x = \int_{X}\phi\chi_Adg_x= L^\infty(g)(\phi)\chi_A(x)$, the result follows. Note that, in the last equality we used a non trivial fact about Markov kernels, indeed, for a disintegration (in general, for an hypothesis), it is true that the function $g_x(B)$ is $\nu$- a.e. equivalent to 0 out of $B$ (because our function $f$ is the identity), so that it is true that $\int_X \varphi \chi_A dg_x$ is a.e. zero outside of $A$, i.e. $\int_X\varphi \chi_A dg_x =_{\nu} \int_A \phi dg_x \chi_A$ and this implies that $\|L^\infty(g)(\varphi\chi'_A)-L^\infty(g)(\varphi)\chi_A\|_\infty = \|L^\infty(g)(\varphi\chi'_A)-L^\infty(g)(\varphi\chi'_A)\chi_A+ L^\infty(g)(\varphi\chi'_A)\chi_A-L^\infty(g)(\varphi)\chi_A\|_\infty\leq \|L^\infty(g)(\varphi\chi'_A)-L^\infty(g)(\varphi\chi'_A)\chi_A\|_\infty + \| L^\infty(g)(\varphi\chi'_A)\chi_A-L^\infty(g)(\varphi)\chi_A\|_\infty $ and then $\|L^\infty(g)(\varphi\chi'_A)-L^\infty(g)(\varphi\chi'_A)\chi_A\|_\infty=0$ because of the above mentioned fact and $ \| L^\infty(g)(\varphi\chi'_A)\chi_A-L^\infty(g)(\varphi)\chi_A\|_\infty =0$ for the same reason (just apply linearity of $L^\infty(g)$ and use the same result). This implies also that nonnegative functions are sent to nonnegative functions, so the map is also positive.\\

We have proved that $L^\infty(g)$ is a conditional expectation and so, because it preserves the states and because tracial states have trivial modular groups, applying the result from Takesaki, we have that $L^\infty(g)$ is the 'probabilistic' unique conditional expectation between the couple $(X,\Sigma,\mu)\supset(X,\Lambda,\nu)$.\\
